HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 stream contract

The proposed endpoint adapter tracks an HTTP message across split frames, repeated packets and interleaved streams. One request stream can carry informational responses before a final response. It identifies the frontend or backend leg explicitly. Existing catalog hooks include tcp.data, quic.initial, quic.crypto_hello, quic.stream, http.request and http.response. The names and types below describe a proposed extension. Decoded HTTP fields require access to plaintext and the connection’s decoding context. Modifying those fields requires an authorized endpoint that owns the outgoing leg.

From wire bytes to field sections

HTTP/2 over TCP
Feed the ordered plaintext byte stream into a 9-byte frame-header parser. Validate the 24-bit length against the permitted frame size before buffering. A TCP segment or TLS record can contain part of a frame or several frames. A missing TCP byte delays all later bytes on that connection, including other HTTP streams. Track stream IDs and half-closures independently. RFC 9113 §4
HTTP/3 over QUIC
The owned QUIC endpoint authenticates packets and reassembles STREAM bytes by connection, stream ID, sending direction and offset. Deliver contiguous bytes once. Consistent overlaps add no new bytes; conflicting data or inconsistent final sizes are transport errors under the applicable QUIC rules. FIN establishes a final size; notify completion only after all preceding bytes arrive. Parse HTTP/3 frame type and length as separate variable-length integers. A gap on one stream leaves others independently deliverable, subject to shared congestion, credit and decoder dependencies. RFC 9000 §2.2 · RFC 9114 §7
Handshake bytes and acknowledgments
QUIC CRYPTO uses its own offset space per direction and encryption level. Initial, Handshake and 1-RTT can carry CRYPTO; 0-RTT cannot. ACK ranges identify received packets within a packet-number space. A transport ACK proves neither HTTP decoding nor application processing. Treat replayable early requests explicitly; application acceptance needs an application signal. RFC 9001 §4 · RFC 8470
Compression belongs to a connection direction
HPACK has one decoder context per sending direction. Process field blocks in wire order, including discarded streams when necessary to maintain context. HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE without END_HEADERS requires contiguous CONTINUATION frames on that stream. QPACK uses separate encoder/decoder instruction streams. A field section can wait for its required insert count while other sections proceed. Bound blocked streams and table capacity by negotiated limits; decode through the owning compression context. RFC 7541 · RFC 9204

Proposed typed interface and commit points

Stream = { connectionGeneration, leg, protocol: H2|H3, streamID }
Message = { stream: Stream, direction, role: Request|Response, ordinal }
Field = { name: Bytes, value: Bytes, sensitive: Bool }
http.fields_ready(Message, phase: Initial|Informational|Final|Trailers,
                  fields: List<Field>) → Observe
http.body_chunk(Message, offset: UInt64, bytes: BoundedBytes) → Observe
http.message_end(Message, bodyBytes: UInt64) → Observe
http.message_aborted(Message, origin, reason, deliveredBytes) → Observe
http.before_send(Message, phase, draft: OwnedFieldSection) → Keep|Replace|Reject
http.datagram_received(Stream, context: Optional<UInt64>, bytes: BoundedBytes) → Observe

Emit fields after complete decompression and HTTP validation. Preserve repeated fields and their order; validate pseudo-fields separately. On the response direction emit each permitted 1xx, then one final response; 101 is unavailable on these protocols. Stream body bytes incrementally with offsets excluding frame headers and padding. Emit trailers once when present. End once per completed message after END_STREAM (HTTP/2) or ordered stream FIN (HTTP/3), including body-length checks where applicable. A reset terminates an incomplete direction with an abort. RFC 9113 §8 · RFC 9114 §4

Only an owned outgoing draft can be changed before encoding. Validate field syntax, pseudo-fields, body framing and length on commit. Serialize through that leg’s encoder. After headers are committed, rejection requires cancellation or another operation legal in the current phase. A successful CONNECT opens a bidirectional tunnel after the final 2xx headers; route subsequent bytes to the tunnel consumer. Extended CONNECT additionally requires negotiated support. HTTP/2 push associates PUSH_PROMISE with a promised stream; HTTP/3 uses a Push ID and a separate unidirectional push stream, within granted push credit. RFC 8441 · RFC 9220 · RFC 9114 §4.6

Cancellation, capacity and failure scope

  • Drain. HTTP/2 GOAWAY gives the highest peer stream ID that might have been processed. An HTTP/3 server gives the first rejected client request stream ID; a client gives the first rejected Push ID. Later GOAWAY cutoffs cannot increase. Track completed, rejected and indeterminate work separately when deciding whether a request can be retried. RFC 9113 §6.8 · RFC 9114 §5.2
  • Cancel. HTTP/2 RST_STREAM closes the stream. QUIC RESET_STREAM aborts the sending direction and declares its final size; STOP_SENDING asks the peer to stop its sending direction. Track both halves and suppress duplicate terminal events. Already delivered application bytes remain accounted for. RFC 9000 §3.5
  • Separate credit from memory. HTTP/2 connection and stream windows count DATA payload including padding. QUIC MAX_DATA and MAX_STREAM_DATA constrain stream offset consumption, including final sizes; retransmissions consume no extra credit. Separately bound partial headers, decoded field bytes/count, QPACK blocked sections, buffered body bytes, gaps, active streams and idle age. Use backpressure; skip unknown frames incrementally where permitted. RFC 9113 §5.2 · RFC 9000 §4
  • Unreliable HTTP/3 datagrams. With negotiated HTTP Datagrams and QUIC DATAGRAM support, demultiplex by Quarter Stream ID to the associated request. Interpret any context identifier according to its application protocol. Delivery may be lost, reordered or duplicated; datagrams have no stream offset, retransmission guarantee or stream flow credit. Apply independent size, rate and queue bounds. RFC 9297 · RFC 9221
  • Contain errors at the specified scope. Invalid HTTP fields or an inconsistent message length generally fail the affected stream. An interleaved HTTP/2 continuation sequence or broken HPACK context fails the connection. An HTTP/3 framing violation, QPACK decompression failure or closed critical stream fails the connection with the applicable error. QUIC flow-control or final-size violations are connection-level transport failures. Distinguish incomplete input, local quota exhaustion and malformed peer input; preserve unrelated streams whenever protocol state permits. RFC 9113 §5.4 · RFC 9114 §8

Where does a gRPC message end?

After HTTP decoding, a gRPC stream still has its own framing. Each message starts with a compression flag and a four-byte big-endian length. This example feeds the same three identity-encoded messages to a parser in different chunk sizes. The middle message has an empty payload. All three belong to one response on one HTTP stream.

Ordered deliveryDecoder stateNew message events

Buffer the prefix and track remaining bytes on the message’s stream. Reserve a bounded payload budget before assembly. For a compressed message, bound decompressed output separately. A complete message can precede a failed RPC. Final trailers or a terminal error determine the RPC outcome.

Which VPN owns a connection, and which backend owns a request?

A browser can send several HTTP requests over one HTTP/2 TCP connection or one HTTP/3 QUIC connection. When the laptop runs the service, the remote client can do the same. Routing a request independently requires an HTTP endpoint that owns the client-facing session and can create a separate upstream request.

Shipping paths and offline fixtures

  • Shared WireGuard router. Its outbound rules can match a visible TCP ClientHello or recognize a QUIC v1/v2 Initial header and read its version and destination connection ID. The router pins a flow to a member and generation. Return traffic must match established reverse state. A QUIC path change can produce a new UDP tuple. A connection ID alone grants neither a route nor admission for that tuple.
  • Proxy Tunnel. On configured TCP ports a visible ClientHello can select a numeric backend before the upstream dial. The proxy relays the original TLS bytes to that backend. Every HTTP/2 stream inside that TLS session follows it. The upstream HTTP(S) proxy mode uses HTTP/1.1 CONNECT. That mode and routed SSH refuse non-DNS UDP. A capable SOCKS5 UDP relay can carry opaque HTTP/3 traffic.
  • Atlas fixtures. http.request, http.response, tls.negotiated and quic.stream accept evidence supplied by a modeled endpoint. A passive packet trace cannot supply encrypted request headers, authenticated principals, RPC status or WebTransport session membership. An incomplete or protected hello leaves the corresponding name unknown.

Proposed decisions at a cooperating HTTP gateway

Two origins on one connection
A browser opens TLS for reports.example, then uses a second stream for payroll.example. Verify the effective scheme and authority on every request, including its port, then check the authenticated caller’s permission for that origin. Reject malformed or conflicting authority information. The client may coalesce origins when its certificate and HTTP authority checks allow it. An ORIGIN frame describes the sender’s claimed origin set. A shared certificate, IP address, SNI or ORIGIN advertisement cannot grant payroll access. Send an authorized reports request through Work and an authorized payroll request through Finance only if the gateway owns both frontend authorities and both upstream routes.
Backend reuse across VPNs or identities
Key reusable backend connections by approved origin and endpoint, VPN member and generation, upstream proxy, TLS verification policy and negotiated protocol, and the security context used on that connection. A Work connection authenticated with one client certificate cannot serve a Finance request merely because both reach the same private IP. Recheck authorization for every new stream. On revocation or a member restart, stop opening affected streams and apply the revocation policy to in-flight work. Confine proxy credentials and header-compression state to their hop. A redirect to a different authority requires a fresh routing and credential decision before forwarding.
A gRPC subscription shares a connection with a payroll update
After decoding the request headers, map the authorized service and method to a backend. Keep the RPC’s messages, flow control, deadline, cancellation and final grpc-status with that request. A bidirectional subscription carries data both ways while the caller and service keep their roles. An upstream stream number belongs to its own connection. HTTP 200 alone does not establish RPC success.
A WebTransport meeting opens streams and sends datagrams
For WebTransport over HTTP/3, authorize the extended CONNECT request, its origin and its authenticated principal. Pin the accepted session to one allowed backend. Associate its child streams and HTTP Datagrams with that session, enforce per-session limits, and release them on close. A datagram can be lost or reordered. Sharing a QUIC connection with another meeting gives neither meeting access to the other’s datagrams.
A backend drains while another request arrives
Stop assigning new requests to that backend connection after GOAWAY. For HTTP/2 the server’s last-stream ID includes the highest client stream it might have processed. For HTTP/3 the server’s cutoff is the first request stream ID it will reject, inclusive. Move a request to an eligible new connection only when its body is replayable and retry policy permits it. An ambiguous disconnect after a payroll update may mean the write succeeded. Report the uncertainty or reconcile it with an application idempotency key.
A resumed TLS session carries early data
TLS 1.3 early data can be replayed. A gateway can defer replay-sensitive operations until the handshake completes or return HTTP 425 Too Early before forwarding them. Authenticate and authorize again on the eventual request. Retry outside early data only when the request body and application policy permit it.

Protocol design reference

Start with the message an adapter can recognize. Use an event when an operation becomes distinguishable, an object for evidence that lives beyond the callback, and a rule action for an effect the owner can still perform.

This is one possible path. HTTP/2 multiplexes requests on streams. SSH can carry another SSH connection. A DNS answer may explain a later connection without becoming one of its parent layers. Each observation keeps its leg, owner and lifetime.

Event, object and command conventions
Choose the trigger
State what became observable and when. A SYN arriving, an OS listener accepting, and a proxy opening its backend socket are three triggers. Record the producer, ingress or egress direction, observation time, member and generation. For a general hook and its refinement, dispatch in that order on the same observation and stop on a terminal decision. Later independent observations have their own dispatch.
Choose the object lifetime
A packet owns its header view. A leg owns transport sequence space. A TLS endpoint owns negotiated keys and peer identity. A multiplexed stream owns its request. A transaction owns its correlation key, deadline and reply state. Keep joins explicit through a parent, related-flow expectation or evidence record. A sequence number or request ID needs its connection, stream or peer scope.
Keep roles distinct
Local and remote describe the observing Mac. Client and server describe a particular protocol exchange. Packet source and destination describe this direction only. An FTP server can initiate an active data connection. A VPN member can carry traffic in either direction. A reverse SSH forward adds a fresh Mac-to-service socket after a remote client connects.
Represent absence
In the current DSL a missing field read raises an evaluation error and table lookup has explicit found and missing cases. For proposed adapters, return a typed availability result for optional observations, with reasons such as encrypted, truncated, unsupported or ambiguous. A present zero port, empty value or false flag remains a value. Tag correlated evidence with its origin, scope and expiry.
Separate three kinds of command
A wire command such as SMTP STARTTLS is input. A handler subscription names the recognized operation. A rule action asks the owning adapter for an effect. A STARTTLS request becomes a protocol transition only after the appropriate positive response. A failed upgrade and a successful handshake produce different observations.
Stage effects before commitment
The typed runtime already has drop(), proxy.select_backend(...) and session.expect(...) in their documented event scopes. The proposed services add operations such as declining a request on an owned frontend, replacing a field in an uncommitted message or canceling a single stream. Each capability needs an explicit result and a commit point. An observer can count or annotate. Rebuilding a message or replying requires ownership of its framing, authentication and state.
Handle duplicates, loss and teardown
Count packet arrivals separately from decoded operations and handler entries. Preserve retransmissions in wire counters. Deduplicate semantic completions with a protocol-specific key where the protocol permits it. Track refusal, parse failure, timeout, cancellation, half-close, expiry and replacement of the owning generation. Bound parser work, outstanding requests, fragments and related-flow expectations.
Compile for the active subscriptions
The shared router already checks for selected DNS, QUIC or ClientHello handlers before parsing that evidence. For new adapters, compile subscriptions into per-owner, per-phase dispatch lists. Activate a higher-layer parser only when a rule or inspection session needs it. Attribute work and errors to their parser and handler. Keep full contents, credentials and payload history out of default counters.

Network and transport

Ethernet
Stack
Link frame carrying an EtherType and payload.
Wire messages or local signals
Unicast, multicast and broadcast frames on an observed interface.
When events fire
Dispatch ethernet.frame for a whole frame at the observation boundary. Direction and interface identify the leg. An adapter that confirms transmission can additionally report a separate completion.
Event vocabulary
ethernet.frame
Objects and lifetimes
Interface, direction, source and destination MAC, EtherType, frame length.
Object field examples
frame.interface, frame.direction, ethernet.type
Actions at the owner
Count by interface or dispatch a validated payload to its EtherType decoder.
Visibility and limits
macOS packet tunnels deliver raw IP. Link headers require a link-layer capture or fixture.
Related catalog hooks
ethernet.frame
802.1Q VLAN
Stack
One or more tags between Ethernet addresses and the payload EtherType.
Wire messages or local signals
A tagged frame carries a VLAN identifier, priority and an encapsulated EtherType.
When events fire
Dispatch vlan.tag for each complete tag, outermost first, scoped to the containing frame and tag index.
Event vocabulary
vlan.tag
Objects and lifetimes
Interface, outer and inner tag indices, VLAN ID, priority, drop eligibility, next EtherType.
Object field examples
vlan.id, vlan.priority, vlan.tag_index
Actions at the owner
Group counters by observed tag and decode the next validated layer.
Visibility and limits
Untagged traffic has no observed tag. Interface offload can remove tags before software sees them.
Related catalog hooks
vlan.tag
ARP
Stack
Ethernet neighbor resolution, usually for IPv4.
Wire messages or local signals
Who-has request, is-at reply, probe and announcement.
When events fire
A complete operation yields arp.request or arp.reply. A neighbor.changed observation requires the local interface owner to confirm a cache change.
Event vocabulary
arp.request Proposed arp.reply Proposed neighbor.changed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Interface, opcode, sender and target protocol and hardware addresses. Optional correlated request.
Object field examples
arp.sender, arp.target, neighbor.interface
Actions at the owner
Count requests and replies separately. Expire a local diagnostic correlation.
Visibility and limits
A sender address is a claim. Announcements and unsolicited replies can arrive without a matching request. Raw IP tunnels omit ARP.
IPv4
Stack
Network-layer datagram over a link or inside an outer tunnel.
Wire messages or local signals
IPv4 header and optional options followed by a payload or one fragment.
When events fire
Dispatch ip.packet and ipv4.packet at the validated packet boundary. A fragment observation records offset and flags. Reassembly owns a separate completion.
Event vocabulary
ip.packet ipv4.packet ip.fragment_seen Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Capture boundary, source, destination, protocol, TTL, DSCP/ECN, length, ID, byte offset, more-fragments bit.

ip.src, ip.dst, ipv4.fragment_offset
Actions at the owner
Classify by destination prefix, count by direction, or apply supported traffic-class changes before forwarding.
Visibility and limits
A later fragment generally lacks the transport header. Seeing one fragment does not establish a complete datagram.
Related catalog hooks
ip.packet ipv4.packet

Stack
Network-layer packet with a fixed header and an optional extension chain.
Wire messages or local signals
Base header, bounded extension headers, optional Fragment header and upper-layer payload.

Inspect visible fields, stop at an opaque next header, and account for unsupported extension chains.

IP fragment reassembly

Optional state between IPv4 or IPv6 fragment input and upper-layer parsing.

Security and tunnels

TLS
Stack
Record and handshake layer over a reliable stream. A separate session per terminated leg.
Wire messages or local signals
ClientHello, ServerHello, Finished, application data and alerts.
When events fire
A complete visible ClientHello yields tls.client_hello when its required metadata is available. The endpoint reports tls.negotiated after its handshake completes. A close belongs to that session and leg.
Event vocabulary
tls.client_hello tls.negotiated tls.closed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Leg and peer role, visible outer name, offered protocols, negotiated version and ALPN, explicit peer-verification result.
Object field examples
tls.sni, tls.version, tls.alpn, tls.peer_verified
Actions at the owner
Select a backend before dialing or set SNI on an independently owned backend TLS client. Retain peer verification on that leg.
Visibility and limits
A passthrough observer cannot read encrypted application records. ECH can hide the inner name, and each TLS leg has its own negotiation.
Related catalog hooks
tls.client_hello tls.negotiated tls.backend_connect

dtls.flight_seen when an observer has the visible records for a flight. dtls.session_ready or dtls.record_accepted only after endpoint validation.
Event vocabulary
dtls.flight_seen Proposed dtls.session_ready Proposed dtls.record_accepted Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Association and direction, version, visible record metadata, endpoint epoch, peer-verification result and optional negotiated connection ID.
Object field examples
dtls.session, dtls.epoch, dtls.record_number
Actions at the owner
Track retransmissions separately from new handshake state and count authenticated endpoint records.
Visibility and limits
Handshake messages can fragment and reorder. Header visibility varies by DTLS version. A generic TLS-over-stream parser cannot decode these datagrams.
WireGuard
Stack
Encrypted layer-3 tunnel over UDP with per-peer state.
Wire messages or local signals
Handshake initiation/response, cookie reply and encrypted transport data, including keepalives.
When events fire
Use wireguard.handshake for the observed peer handshake status. A subsequent authenticated inner packet is a separate observation after decryption and peer admission.
Event vocabulary
wireguard.handshake wireguard.peer wireguard.inner_received Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Profile and peer generation, allowed prefixes, latest handshake age, directional counters and an admitted inner packet.
Object field examples
wireguard.handshake_age, wireguard.allowed_prefix, flow.generation
Actions at the owner
Attribute counters to a configured peer and enforce its allowed destinations or source prefixes at the appropriate boundary.
Visibility and limits
An outer UDP datagram gives no proof of successful authentication. Roaming can change the peer endpoint while the configured peer remains the same.
Related catalog hooks
wireguard.handshake wireguard.peer
IKEv2
Stack
Control plane that authenticates peers and negotiates IPsec security associations.
Wire messages or local signals
IKE_SA_INIT, IKE_AUTH, CREATE_CHILD_SA and INFORMATIONAL request/response exchanges.
When events fire
ike.exchange_completed on a matching validated response at the owning IKE endpoint. ike.child_installed when the endpoint installs negotiated child SAs.
Event vocabulary
ike.state ike.exchange_completed Proposed ike.child_installed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Profile generation, exchange type, message ID, initiator/responder SPIs and endpoint-owned SA generation.
Object field examples
ike.exchange, ike.message_id, ike.child
Actions at the owner
Observe connection state, correlate owned exchange outcomes and record rekeys separately from new profile connections.
Visibility and limits
Apple personal VPN exposes connection status to this app. Detailed exchanges, encrypted authentication details and SA installation are endpoint-only.
Related catalog hooks
ike.state
IPsec ESP and AH
Stack
IP-layer security associations, in transport or tunnel mode. ESP can use UDP encapsulation.
Wire messages or local signals
ESP secured packets and AH authenticated packets. Separate unidirectional SAs carry inbound and outbound traffic.
When events fire
ipsec.packet_accepted after the owning inbound SA authenticates and admits a packet. ipsec.sa_replaced when a new directional SA supersedes an older one.
Event vocabulary
ipsec.sa ipsec.packet_accepted Proposed ipsec.sa_replaced Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
SA direction, protocol, destination, SPI, transform and generation. Authenticated inner headers depend on mode and endpoint access.
Object field examples
ipsec.spi, ipsec.direction, ipsec.transform
Actions at the owner
Count accepted bytes per SA and forward inner traffic only after the owning endpoint’s checks.
Visibility and limits
An SPI alone is insufficient to identify a global peer or prove acceptance. Apple personal VPN hides its SA table. The SA hook is an endpoint fixture.
Related catalog hooks
ipsec.sa
L2TP/IPsec
Stack
PPP frames carried by an L2TPv2 session inside IPsec.
Wire messages or local signals
Tunnel and session control messages, PPP link negotiation, encapsulated PPP data, disconnect and tunnel stop.
When events fire
l2tp.session_ready when the owning L2TP endpoint establishes the session. ppp.network_ready per negotiated network-control protocol.
Event vocabulary
l2tp.state l2tp.session_ready Proposed ppp.network_ready Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Profile generation, directional tunnel/session identifiers, PPP protocol and assigned address if reported.
Object field examples
l2tp.session_id, ppp.family, ipsec.spi
Actions at the owner
Report session state and publish negotiated routes or addresses from authorized endpoint callbacks.
Visibility and limits
IPsec observers cannot inspect the protected L2TP exchange. SimpleVPN exports the L2TP configuration. An external owner manages the resulting session.
Related catalog hooks
l2tp.state
OpenVPN
Stack
VPN control and data channels over UDP or TCP.
Wire messages or local signals
Control-channel negotiation, authentication result, tunnel configuration, protected data and rekey.
When events fire
openvpn.configuration_ready when the engine delivers validated tunnel configuration. openvpn.data_key_changed on an owned data-channel key-generation change.
Event vocabulary
openvpn.connected openvpn.configuration_ready Proposed openvpn.data_key_changed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Profile generation, engine status, assigned addresses, route proposals and negotiated transport where reported.
Object field examples
vpn.profile, vpn.generation, openvpn.key_generation
Actions at the owner
Apply authorized route proposals and track a reconnect as a new generation.
Visibility and limits
A transport connection alone does not indicate completed VPN authentication or a configured tunnel. Session credentials stay within the engine.
Related catalog hooks
openvpn.connected vpn.state
OpenConnect
Stack
One client library for several vendor SSL VPN protocols and data transports.
Wire messages or local signals
Gateway negotiation, authentication result, tunnel configuration, optional data-channel upgrade and disconnect.
When events fire
openconnect.transport_changed when the owning engine confirms a data-transport transition. openconnect.configuration_ready on a delivered configuration.
Event vocabulary
openconnect.connected openconnect.transport_changed Proposed openconnect.configuration_ready Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Profile generation, gateway protocol family, assigned address, routes and current transport where reported.
Object field examples
openconnect.protocol, vpn.generation, openconnect.transport
Actions at the owner
Apply validated configuration and record fallback or reconnection as reported by the engine.
Visibility and limits
Cisco, Fortinet, F5, GlobalProtect, Juniper, Pulse and Array use different exchanges. Authentication cookies and submitted credentials stay private.
Related catalog hooks
openconnect.connected vpn.state
Tailscale
Stack
Local mesh node with a coordination plane and encrypted peer data paths.
Wire messages or local signals
Node state and network-map updates, route advertisements, direct peer traffic and encrypted relay traffic.
When events fire
tailscale.netmap_updated on an accepted control update. tailscale.path_changed when the owning node confirms a direct or relayed peer path.
Event vocabulary
tailscale.state tailscale.netmap_updated Proposed tailscale.path_changed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Node/profile generation, backend state, assigned addresses, peer-scoped path and authorized routes.
Object field examples
tailscale.backend_state, tailscale.peer, tailscale.path
Actions at the owner
Refresh scoped route proposals, withdraw superseded generations and report local node state.
Visibility and limits
Control service reachability and a particular peer’s data-path reachability are independent. A relay transports encrypted peer data.
Related catalog hooks
tailscale.state route.advertised route.withdrawn
Headscale
Stack
Self-hosted coordination service used by the Tailscale-compatible local node.
Wire messages or local signals
Registration and map updates through coordination. Peer data follows the local node’s direct or relay path.
When events fire
Use the common Tailscale node events for an accepted netmap and a confirmed path change. The configured control provider is a property of that node.
Event vocabulary
headscale.state tailscale.netmap_updated Proposed tailscale.path_changed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Profile generation, configured control-server scope, local backend state, assigned prefixes and advertised routes.
Object field examples
tailscale.backend_state, vpn.profile, tailscale.control_server
Actions at the owner
Attribute state to the selected profile and apply or withdraw route proposals by generation.
Visibility and limits
The coordination server is separate from a traffic relay. A local node status event alone cannot establish individual peer reachability.
Related catalog hooks
headscale.state route.advertised route.withdrawn
VPN lifecycle and route ownership
Stack
Local control-plane state across VPN profiles and tunnel generations.
Wire messages or local signals
Start, connecting, connected, stop and disconnect observations. Member route proposals and withdrawals.
When events fire
vpn.generation_started after the owner accepts a start. route.installed after a validated proposal commits. route.removed when that owner releases the prefix.
Event vocabulary
vpn.state route.advertised route.withdrawn route.installed Proposed route.removed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Profile, generation, member, prefix and family, default-route flag, metric and install outcome.
Object field examples
vpn.generation, route.member, route.prefix
Actions at the owner
Validate eligible prefixes, retain or replace ownership deliberately, and ignore a stale withdrawal from an earlier generation.
Visibility and limits
A proposal, a committed route and a successful data transfer are separate observations. A profile connected callback authenticates no unrelated flow.
Related catalog hooks
vpn.state route.advertised route.withdrawn

Naming and discovery

DNS over UDP
Stack
DNS over UDP/IP · RFC 1035
Wire messages or local signals
A client sends a question. A reply can contain records, a referral, a negative answer or the truncation flag.
When events fire
A resolver parses a complete question. On a response from the expected peer, correlate the ID and question before recording answers or requesting a TCP retry.
Event vocabulary
dns.query dns.answer dns.transaction_expired Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Resolver, VPN/source scope, transaction ID, question name/type/class, response code, record TTL in seconds.
Object field examples
dns.id, dns.name, dns.type, dns.ttl, dns.resolver_scope
Actions at the owner
Choose an approved resolver at query time. Cache validated answers within their scope and lifetime.
Visibility and limits
A DNS answer alone grants no egress to the returned address. Encrypted DNS has a separate transport boundary.
Related catalog hooks
dns.query dns.answer udp.datagram
DNS over TCP
Stack
Length-prefixed DNS over a TCP byte stream · RFC 7766
Wire messages or local signals
A two-octet length precedes each DNS message. A connection may carry pipelined queries and responses in a different order.
When events fire
Emit a parsed question or answer only after the full declared message arrives. Match outstanding transactions within the connection.
Event vocabulary
dns.query dns.answer dns.transaction_expired Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Connection generation, message length, DNS ID, question, response code and scoped records.
Object field examples
dns.id, dns.name, dns.connection, dns.resolver_scope
Actions at the owner
A DNS endpoint may retry a truncated UDP query over TCP or reuse a connection to its approved resolver.
Visibility and limits
TCP segment boundaries do not delimit DNS messages. The current outbound DNS packet hook parses UDP questions.
Related catalog hooks
tcp.data dns.query dns.answer
DNS over TLS (DoT)
Stack
DNS framing over TLS over TCP · RFC 7858
Wire messages or local signals
Establish TLS with the resolver, then exchange length-prefixed DNS questions and replies inside that session.
When events fire
Report the negotiated transport at the TLS owner. Emit each DNS transaction when its plaintext message has been reassembled.
Event vocabulary
tls.negotiated dns.query dns.answer
Objects and lifetimes
Resolver identity and verification, TLS session, DNS connection and transaction, per-record TTL.
Object field examples
tls.peer_verified, tls.version, dns.name, dns.resolver_scope
Actions at the owner
Select a configured DoT endpoint before dialing. Apply query or cache policy at the terminating resolver client.
Visibility and limits
A packet observer can sometimes see a ClientHello. Seeing it does not expose the DNS questions.
Related catalog hooks
tls.client_hello tls.negotiated dns.query dns.answer
DNS over HTTPS (DoH)
Stack
DNS wire format inside an HTTP request and response over TLS · RFC 8484
Wire messages or local signals
A GET encodes a query in the dns parameter. A POST transports the DNS wire message in its body. An HTTP success can still contain a DNS error.
When events fire
At the HTTP endpoint, validate the request format, then parse one complete DNS message. Associate its response with that HTTP exchange.
Event vocabulary
http.request dns.query dns.answer http.response
Objects and lifetimes
Resolver URI, HTTP stream or request, HTTP status, DNS response code and record lifetime.
Object field examples
http.content_type, http.stream_id, dns.name, dns.resolver_scope
Actions at the owner
Choose the configured DoH resolver and respect DNS expiry and HTTP cache age when reusing a response.
Visibility and limits
The query name can be sensitive even in a GET URI. An HTTPS relay sees protected bytes unless it terminates that session.
Related catalog hooks
http.request http.response dns.query dns.answer
DNS over QUIC (DoQ)
Stack
Length-prefixed DNS over QUIC over UDP · RFC 9250
Wire messages or local signals
A client opens a bidirectional QUIC stream for a query. Its response travels on that stream. Independent queries use independent streams.
When events fire
At the DoQ endpoint, require negotiated doq and a complete DNS frame. Correlate by stream and process transfer responses under their protocol rules.
Event vocabulary
quic.stream dns.query dns.answer
Objects and lifetimes
QUIC connection and stream, resolver identity, message length and DNS records. DoQ sets the DNS message ID to zero.
Object field examples
quic.stream_id, dns.name, dns.type, dns.resolver_scope
Actions at the owner
Enforce per-stream deadlines and limits at the DoQ endpoint. Reuse the authenticated resolver connection.
Visibility and limits
A public QUIC Initial header does not reveal DNS messages. UDP five-tuples can change during a QUIC connection.
Related catalog hooks
quic.initial quic.stream dns.query dns.answer
Multicast DNS (mDNS)
Stack
Link-local multicast DNS over UDP · RFC 6762
Wire messages or local signals
A querier asks on an interface. Multiple responders can answer. Probes, announcements, known-answer suppression and TTL-zero goodbyes affect the local cache.
When events fire
Record a scoped record after validating the received message and link. Apply cache-flush and goodbye timing for the applicable record set.
Event vocabulary
dns.query mdns.record_seen Proposed mdns.record_expired Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Interface generation, address family, name/type/class, responder, cache-flush bit and TTL.
Object field examples
mdns.interface, mdns.record, mdns.cache_flush
Actions at the owner
An mDNS service can publish local records or expire cached records. Relay between interfaces only under explicit bridge policy.
Visibility and limits
Link-local names and duplicate responders prevent a global name-to-IP binding. The ordinary unicast DNS packet hook is not an mDNS adapter.
Related catalog hooks
udp.datagram
DNS-Based Service Discovery (DNS-SD)
Stack
DNS resource records over unicast DNS or mDNS · RFC 6763
Wire messages or local signals
A PTR enumerates service instances. SRV supplies a target and port, TXT describes the instance, and A/AAAA can resolve the target.
When events fire
Emit a browsed instance when the scoped PTR appears. Resolve an endpoint when the selected instance has a valid SRV and usable address.
Event vocabulary
dnssd.instance_seen Proposed dnssd.endpoint_resolved Proposed dnssd.instance_expired Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Browse domain and interface, service type, instance name, SRV priority/weight/port, target, optional TXT and record expiries.
Object field examples
dnssd.instance, dnssd.service_type, dnssd.target, dnssd.port
Actions at the owner
An owned browser may present instances or connect to a chosen, independently authorized endpoint.
Visibility and limits
TXT can contain private or untrusted text. DNS-SD is a record model and also works with ordinary unicast DNS.
Related catalog hooks
dns.query dns.answer
DHCPv4
Stack
BOOTP-format DHCP over IPv4/UDP · RFC 2131
Wire messages or local signals
A client can discover, receive offers, request a lease and receive ACK or NAK. Renew and rebind are later exchanges. Release ends a lease.
When events fire
At the DHCP client, accept a reply matching its state, transaction, interface and server selection. Report acquisition, renewal, expiry or rejection.
Event vocabulary
dhcp.offer Proposed dhcp.ack Proposed lease.installed Proposed lease.expired Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Interface, transaction ID, client and server identity, offered IPv4 address, lease time and approved options.
Object field examples
dhcp.xid, lease.address, lease.interface, lease.expires
Actions at the owner
The interface’s DHCP owner may install a validated address, router and DNS settings, then remove them on expiry.
Visibility and limits
An offer or captured ACK cannot alter a VPN member or install host routes. The OS owns the physical interface lease.
Related catalog hooks
ipv4.packet udp.datagram
DHCPv6
Stack
DHCPv6 over IPv6/UDP, optionally relayed · RFC 9915
Wire messages or local signals
Solicit, Advertise, Request and Reply select addresses or delegated prefixes. Rapid Commit and stateless Information-request have different sequences.
When events fire
At the client, correlate the exchange, client/server IDs and identity association. Report delegated prefixes and preferred/valid lifetime changes separately.
Event vocabulary
dhcpv6.advertise Proposed dhcpv6.reply Proposed lease.installed Proposed lease.expired Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Interface and relay context, transaction ID, DUID, IAID, address or prefix, preferred/valid lifetimes in seconds.
Object field examples
dhcpv6.transaction, dhcpv6.iaid, lease.prefix
Actions at the owner
An authorized client or delegating router can apply the validated lease or delegated prefix and withdraw it when it expires.
Visibility and limits
An IPv6 default router comes from Router Advertisements. DUIDs and delegated prefixes should stay scoped to their link or client.
Related catalog hooks
ipv6.packet udp.datagram
Network Time Protocol (NTP)
Stack
NTPv4 over UDP · RFC 5905
Wire messages or local signals
In client/server mode the request supplies a transmit timestamp. The reply echoes it as origin time and supplies server receive and transmit times. The client measures local arrival.
When events fire
At the time client, correlate the reply and validate its mode, state and timestamps before deriving a delay or offset sample.
Event vocabulary
ntp.request Proposed ntp.sample_matched Proposed ntp.sample_accepted Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Peer association, poll epoch, stratum, leap state, origin/receive/transmit/destination times and local sample uncertainty.
Object field examples
ntp.peer, ntp.origin_time, ntp.stratum
Actions at the owner
A time daemon may accept or discard a sample, compare multiple sources and discipline its own clock.
Visibility and limits
Packet timing alone does not establish reliable wall time. Clock control belongs to the system time service.
Related catalog hooks
udp.datagram
Network Time Security (NTS)
Stack
NTS key establishment over TLS/TCP, followed by authenticated NTP/UDP · RFC 8915
Wire messages or local signals
NTS-KE negotiates algorithms and delivers cookies. Later NTP requests and replies carry extension fields and authentication evidence.
When events fire
After authenticated NTS-KE, bind the negotiated NTP endpoint to the association. Accept timing samples only after validating the response and request identifier.
Event vocabulary
tls.negotiated nts.association_ready Proposed ntp.sample_accepted Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Verified key-establishment peer, negotiated NTP endpoint, association generation and authentication result. Keep keys and cookies private.
Object field examples
nts.association, nts.server, ntp.peer
Actions at the owner
The owned NTS client may refresh its association and reject unverifiable samples before its clock selection policy runs.
Visibility and limits
TLS protects the setup connection. The subsequent NTP packets have their own authentication and lifetime.
Related catalog hooks
tls.negotiated udp.datagram

Web and remote access

HTTP/1.1
Stack
HTTP messages on an ordered byte stream, optionally over TLS · RFC 9110 and RFC 9112
Wire messages or local signals
A request line and fields precede an optional framed body. Informational responses can precede a final response. A successful CONNECT or negotiated Upgrade changes subsequent framing.
When events fire
A terminating HTTP parser emits a request after valid headers and a complete-response event according to method, status and message framing.
Event vocabulary
http.request http.response http.upgraded Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Connection generation, request sequence, method, authority, target, status, byte counts and handoff state.
Object field examples
http.method, http.authority, http.status, http.transaction
Actions at the owner
An HTTP owner may route a permitted request, construct a protocol-correct response or end the connection on invalid framing.
Visibility and limits
Nested HTTPS hides messages from an outer tunnel. Keep credentials and query-string values out of routine inspection.
Related catalog hooks
http.request http.response http.connect
HTTP/2
Stack
HTTP semantics on multiplexed HTTP/2 streams over TCP, commonly TLS with h2 · RFC 9113
Wire messages or local signals
SETTINGS configures a connection. HEADERS, DATA and trailers carry a request or response. RST_STREAM ends a stream and GOAWAY constrains new work.
When events fire
Emit request metadata only after HPACK header completion. Associate interim/final responses, end-of-stream and resets with the correct stream.
Event vocabulary
http.request http.response http.stream_reset Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Connection, stream ID, decoded pseudo-fields, end-of-stream, reset cause and flow-control state.
Object field examples
http.stream_id, http.authority, http.transaction, http.status
Actions at the owner
A terminating proxy can route or reject one request stream and apply stream-level backpressure.
Visibility and limits
TCP segments and HTTP/2 frames can split a header block. One pooled connection may serve many requests or authorities.
Related catalog hooks
http.request http.response tcp.data tls.negotiated
HTTP/3
Stack
HTTP over QUIC/TLS 1.3 over UDP · RFC 9114 and RFC 9204
Wire messages or local signals
QUIC control streams carry settings. Request streams carry HEADERS and DATA. QPACK decoding can depend on instructions from another stream.
When events fire
At the H3 endpoint emit headers when QPACK dependencies resolve. Record stream completion, cancellation and connection shutdown separately.
Event vocabulary
quic.stream http.request http.response http.stream_reset Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
QUIC connection, request stream ID, method, authority, status, QPACK decoding state and per-stream bytes.
Object field examples
quic.stream_id, http.authority, http.transaction
Actions at the owner
The HTTP/3 owner may select a backend per request or cancel one stream without closing unrelated streams.
Visibility and limits
A QUIC version or connection ID reveals no HTTP method or path. Connection migration can change observed network addresses.
Related catalog hooks
quic.initial quic.stream http.request http.response
HTTP CONNECT and HTTPS proxy
Stack
TCP tunneling through HTTP/1.1 CONNECT or an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 CONNECT stream · RFC 9110
Wire messages or local signals
The client requests a target authority. A final 2xx establishes the tunnel. With an HTTPS proxy an outer TLS connection authenticates the proxy before CONNECT.
When events fire
At the configured proxy owner, emit target requested, final response and tunnel ready or refused. Track any later inner TLS session independently.
Event vocabulary
http.request http.connect proxy.pre_connect http.response
Objects and lifetimes
Proxy identity, client-side stream, requested authority, upstream socket, response status and both leg lifetimes.
Object field examples
http.authority, proxy.target, proxy.port, http.status
Actions at the owner
The proxy may authorize the target, connect it and relay bytes, or return a refusal on the initiating leg.
Visibility and limits
An HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 tunnel owns a stream. HTTP/1.1 switches its connection to tunnel data. Nested TLS remains end to end.
Related catalog hooks
http.connect proxy.pre_connect tls.backend_connect
Extended CONNECT
Stack
Protocol-labeled CONNECT stream in HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 · RFC 8441 and RFC 9220
Wire messages or local signals
After the server advertises extended CONNECT support, the client sends CONNECT with a protocol identifier. A successful response hands that stream to the named protocol.
When events fire
Emit a protocol handoff only after validating the advertised capability, request pseudo-fields and acceptance response.
Event vocabulary
http.request http.connect tunnel.established Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
HTTP connection and stream, protocol identifier, authority/path and accepted inner protocol context.
Object field examples
http.stream_id, http.extended_protocol, tunnel.inner
Actions at the owner
The HTTP endpoint may approve a supported protocol or refuse the request while other streams continue.
Visibility and limits
Ordinary CONNECT and a successful response alone do not identify a WebSocket, UDP tunnel or other inner protocol.
Related catalog hooks
http.connect http.request http.response
MASQUE CONNECT-UDP
Stack
HTTP proxy for a fixed UDP target, using HTTP Datagrams or the DATAGRAM capsule · RFC 9297 and RFC 9298
Wire messages or local signals
An accepted connect-udp request establishes a datagram context. Later HTTP Datagrams carry UDP payloads to or from the negotiated target.
When events fire
At the MASQUE proxy, report accepted target and request context, then datagram relay and closure for that association.
Event vocabulary
http.connect masque.context_ready Proposed udp.datagram
Objects and lifetimes
Proxy connection, HTTP request stream, context ID, target host/port, datagram lengths and association lifetime.
Object field examples
masque.context, proxy.target, udp.length
Actions at the owner
An authorized endpoint may open one scoped UDP association, enforce datagram limits and close it with the tunnel.
Visibility and limits
HTTP/1.1 uses Upgrade. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 use extended CONNECT. The physical peer is the proxy, while the inner UDP target is separate.
Related catalog hooks
http.request http.response udp.owned_datagram
MASQUE CONNECT-IP
Stack
IP packets inside an HTTP proxy tunnel · RFC 9484
Wire messages or local signals
An accepted connect-ip request carries IP packets as HTTP Datagrams. Capsules can assign addresses or advertise reachable routes.
When events fire
Emit address assignment or route advertisement only after decoding the applicable capsule on an authorized tunnel. Independently validate forwarded inner packets.
Event vocabulary
http.connect masque.context_ready Proposed ip.packet
Objects and lifetimes
Tunnel generation and request context, assigned addresses, authorized prefixes, protocol and inner IP tuple.
Object field examples
masque.context, route.prefix, tunnel.inner
Actions at the owner
A CONNECT-IP owner can forward within accepted prefixes and remove tunnel-scoped routes when the context ends.
Visibility and limits
An advertisement is a proposal to routing policy. It cannot silently expand a VPN peer’s authorized networks.
Related catalog hooks
http.request route.advertised route.withdrawn ip.packet
WebSocket
Stack
Framed bidirectional messages over HTTP Upgrade or extended CONNECT · RFC 6455, RFC 8441 and RFC 9220
Wire messages or local signals
HTTP/1.1 upgrades with a validated 101 handshake. H2/H3 use an accepted extended CONNECT stream. Data fragments, ping/pong and close frames follow.
When events fire
At the WebSocket endpoint, emit a message after complete fragment reassembly. Track control frames and each side’s closing state separately.
Event vocabulary
websocket.open Proposed websocket.message Proposed websocket.close Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Connection or stream, negotiated subprotocol/extensions, message opcode, bounded decoded length and close code.
Object field examples
websocket.connection, websocket.opcode, websocket.message_length
Actions at the owner
A terminating service may select a subprotocol, limit message size or close its own WebSocket session.
Visibility and limits
Compressed frames and fragmented messages need bounded decoding. Outer packet sizes cannot identify message boundaries.
Related catalog hooks
http.request http.response quic.stream
gRPC
Stack
gRPC messages and status on HTTP/2 streams · gRPC HTTP/2 protocol specification
Wire messages or local signals
Initial headers identify the service method. Each message has a compression flag and length. Streaming RPCs carry multiple messages. Trailers, or a trailers-only response, report gRPC status.
When events fire
At the gRPC endpoint, report method accepted, each fully framed message, deadline/cancellation and final RPC status separately from HTTP status.
Event vocabulary
http.request grpc.call Proposed grpc.message Proposed grpc.completed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
HTTP stream and RPC, service/method, deadline, compression, message counts, directions and final grpc-status.
Object field examples
grpc.method, grpc.stream, grpc.message_encoding, grpc.status
Actions at the owner
An RPC-aware proxy may route by approved method, enforce size/deadline policy or finish its owned stream with a gRPC status.
Visibility and limits
An HTTP 200 does not imply RPC success. Message contents require their schema and should stay outside routine routing telemetry.
Related catalog hooks
http.request http.response
SOCKS5 CONNECT
Stack
SOCKS5 negotiation and TCP relay · RFC 1928
Wire messages or local signals
Client and proxy negotiate an authentication method. After any authentication, CONNECT identifies a target and the proxy returns a reply before relaying bytes.
When events fire
At an owned SOCKS endpoint, distinguish method selection, authorized target request, final reply and connection closure.
Event vocabulary
socks.request socks.reply tunnel.established Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Proxy session, command, address type, requested target/port, bound address and reply code. Exclude authentication secrets.
Object field examples
socks.command, socks.target, socks.status, socks.bound_port
Actions at the owner
A configured proxy may dial an approved target or return the matching SOCKS refusal.
Visibility and limits
A domain-name target is resolved according to the proxy’s policy. Inner TLS, SSH or other application encryption stays independent.
Related catalog hooks
socks.request socks.reply proxy.pre_connect
SOCKS5 BIND and UDP ASSOCIATE
Stack
SOCKS5 TCP control connection plus an accepted peer or encapsulated UDP relay · RFC 1928
Wire messages or local signals
BIND returns a listen endpoint, then a second reply when an incoming peer connects. UDP ASSOCIATE returns a relay endpoint. Later UDP packets include their own destination header.
When events fire
Model BIND listener readiness and peer acceptance as distinct events. For UDP, associate relay traffic with the originating control connection until it ends.
Event vocabulary
socks.request socks.reply socks.peer_accepted Proposed socks.association_expired Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Control session, command, listener/relay endpoint, allowed client and remote peer. Each UDP message also names an address type and destination.
Object field examples
socks.command, socks.association, socks.bound_address
Actions at the owner
An owned proxy can constrain the accepted peer or relay destination and retire the UDP association when the TCP control connection closes.
Visibility and limits
A successful first BIND reply is not an accepted peer. A UDP association does not grant an unrestricted path through the VPN.
Related catalog hooks
socks.request socks.reply udp.owned_datagram
SSH local forwarding
Stack
Local TCP listener into a direct-tcpip channel on an authenticated SSH transport · RFC 4254
Wire messages or local signals
A connection accepted at the client opens a direct-tcpip channel. The server opens the requested target and confirms or rejects the channel, then exchanges data and closes it.
When events fire
At the SSH owner, confirm host verification and session readiness. Record each channel open, acceptance or failure independently.
Event vocabulary
ssh.session ssh.forward_open ssh.channel_confirmed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
SSH transport generation, local listener, originator, requested target, channel IDs, window and half-close state.
Object field examples
ssh.direction, ssh.target, ssh.port, ssh.channel
Actions at the owner
The SSH endpoint may permit a target, open its own connection and enforce per-channel backpressure.
Visibility and limits
A forwarded channel can contain another encrypted session. External SSH helper modes expose helper lifecycle to SimpleVPN.
Related catalog hooks
ssh.session ssh.forward_open
SSH remote forwarding
Stack
Remote listener negotiated on SSH, then forwarded-tcpip channels back to the client · RFC 4254
Wire messages or local signals
The client requests tcpip-forward. An accepted remote listen request can yield multiple forwarded-tcpip channels as remote peers connect. Cancellation stops future listens.
When events fire
Only report a listener after confirmation. Correlate each incoming channel with the previously authorized remote bind before connecting its configured local target.
Event vocabulary
ssh.listener_ready Proposed ssh.forward_open ssh.channel_confirmed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
SSH session, requested and allocated remote bind, originator, channel and authorized local target.
Object field examples
ssh.listener, ssh.originator, ssh.channel, socket.local_address
Actions at the owner
The SSH owner may accept or reject the listener and each channel, or cancel the forwarding request.
Visibility and limits
The remote peer initiates the data leg. Listener cancellation and the lifetime of already opened channels are distinct.
Related catalog hooks
ssh.session ssh.forward_open
SSH dynamic forwarding
Stack
Local SOCKS listener selecting one SSH direct-tcpip channel per accepted target · RFC 1928 and RFC 4254
Wire messages or local signals
The local proxy decodes the SOCKS request. The SSH client opens the corresponding channel and reports the result to the local client.
When events fire
Correlate the authorized SOCKS CONNECT with a confirmed SSH channel before reporting success or relaying data.
Event vocabulary
socks.request ssh.forward_open ssh.channel_confirmed Proposed socks.reply
Objects and lifetimes
Local SOCKS client and target, verified SSH transport, distinct SSH channel and its target socket.
Object field examples
socks.target, ssh.target, ssh.channel
Actions at the owner
An owned local proxy may constrain destinations, map channel-open failures to SOCKS replies and close only the affected session.
Visibility and limits
This composition does not imply SOCKS BIND or UDP support. External helper ownership can hide the individual channels from the app.
Related catalog hooks
socks.request socks.reply ssh.forward_open
SSH jump hosts (ProxyJump)
Stack
Target SSH transport inside a forwarding channel through a jump host · OpenSSH ProxyJump
Wire messages or local signals
The client establishes SSH to the jump host, obtains TCP forwarding to the target, and negotiates a distinct SSH transport and host key with the target.
When events fire
At the client verify each hop’s identity separately. Associate jump-channel availability with the inner handshake, then track channels on the target session.
Event vocabulary
ssh.session ssh.forward_open ssh.channel_confirmed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Hop or chain index, verified jump peer, transit channel, target endpoint, independently verified target host key and target session.
Object field examples
ssh.transport, ssh.channel, ssh.host_verified
Actions at the owner
A client may select an approved jump path and decline an unexpected host key at either handshake.
Visibility and limits
Successful jump authentication does not authenticate the target. The jump host forwards the inner protected stream.
Related catalog hooks
ssh.session ssh.forward_open

Application services

FTP · active data
Stack
FTP control TCP plus a separate server-initiated data TCP connection.
Wire messages or local signals
PORT or EPRT announces the client listener. A transfer command and preliminary reply precede the data connection. A final reply reports transfer status.
When events fire
Control command parsed → accepted active endpoint → server SYN to client → transfer complete or grant expired.
Event vocabulary
ftp.command ftp.reply ftp.data_offer expectation.consumed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
A control session owns a bounded data expectation tied to its generation, VPN member, peer, direction and authorized listener.
Object field examples
ftp.command, ftp.peer, ftp.port, ftp.control_generation
Actions at the owner
The fixture can reserve one exact related tuple. Consume it once on a matching opening SYN and remove it on parent close or expiry.
Visibility and limits
The shared WireGuard router rejects incoming packets without an existing reverse mapping. Its shipping return path cannot consume this fixture grant.
Related catalog hooks
ftp.command ftp.reply ftp.data_offer tcp.syn
FTP · passive data
Stack
FTP control TCP plus a separate client-initiated data TCP connection.
Wire messages or local signals
PASV supplies a server address and port. EPSV supplies a port on the control peer. The client opens a separate data connection to that listener.
When events fire
Parsed PASV or EPSV dispatches ftp.command, then ftp.command.passive. A later passive reply supplies the port. The approved data connection has its own lifetime.
Event vocabulary
ftp.command ftp.command.passive ftp.reply ftp.data_offer expectation.consumed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
The passive listener belongs to one control session. The data TCP tuple has its own sequence numbers and lifetime.
Object field examples
ftp.command, ftp.code, ftp.mode, ftp.port
Actions at the owner
Keep the data connection on its authorized control member. Bound an expectation to the selected server and port, then discard it after use.
Visibility and limits
The negotiated port has protocol meaning only alongside the matching control exchange. A proposed address needs independent authorization.
Related catalog hooks
ftp.command ftp.command.passive ftp.reply ftp.data_offer tcp.syn
FTPS · private control and data
Stack
FTP over implicit TLS or explicit AUTH TLS. FTP data connections remain separate and may negotiate their own TLS sessions.
Wire messages or local signals
AUTH TLS and a positive response precede an explicit control handshake. PBSZ and PROT select data protection. In implicit mode the control connection starts with TLS.
When events fire
Control TLS negotiated → data protection selected → observable FTP offer at an owning endpoint → separate data handshake if private.
Event vocabulary
ftp.command tls.negotiated ftp.command.passive ftp.data_offer
Objects and lifetimes
One TLS control session can own multiple transfers. Each private data leg has a separate TCP connection and TLS state.
Object field examples
ftp.tls_mode, ftp.control_encrypted, ftp.data_private, tls.version
Actions at the owner
At the protocol endpoint require the intended transport protection, verify peers and associate an approved data leg with its control session.
Visibility and limits
Ordinary passthrough can reveal an outer handshake. FTP commands and passive or active offers inside TLS require a cooperating endpoint.
Related catalog hooks
tls.client_hello tls.negotiated ftp.command ftp.reply ftp.data_offer ftp.command.passive
SMTP · STARTTLS and submission
Stack
SMTP over TCP with explicit STARTTLS or implicit TLS for an appropriately configured submission service.
Wire messages or local signals
Greeting → EHLO → STARTTLS → 220 → TLS → fresh EHLO. MAIL FROM, RCPT TO and DATA belong to a later mail transaction.
When events fire
Proposed endpoint triggers include greeting complete, TLS accepted or refused, post-TLS capabilities available and transaction status returned.
Event vocabulary
smtp.command Proposed smtp.starttls_accepted Proposed tls.negotiated smtp.message_accepted Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
A connection contains capability epochs and successive mail transactions. A transaction has one envelope and potentially many recipients.
Object field examples
smtp.verb, smtp.transaction, smtp.reply_code
Actions at the owner
The submitting client can require verified TLS before authentication or message submission. Count outcomes without retaining addresses or content.
Visibility and limits
An upgrade starts after the positive response. Pre-TLS capability knowledge is discarded. A packet hook cannot read subsequent SMTP replies inside TLS.
Related catalog hooks
tcp.syn tcp.data tls.client_hello tls.negotiated
IMAP · STARTTLS and implicit TLS
Stack
IMAP over TCP with an optional preauthentication STARTTLS exchange or TLS from the first byte.
Wire messages or local signals
A tagged STARTTLS command receives a tagged OK before TLS begins. Recheck CAPABILITY after TLS. SELECT and FETCH operate in an authenticated mailbox.
When events fire
Proposed endpoint triggers include tagged completion, TLS established, mailbox selected and an unsolicited update received during IDLE.
Event vocabulary
imap.command Proposed imap.reply Proposed imap.unsolicited Proposed tls.negotiated
Objects and lifetimes
A connection owns tagged commands, untagged responses and one selected mailbox. A UID is scoped by mailbox and UIDVALIDITY.
Object field examples
imap.tag, imap.mailbox, imap.uid_validity
Actions at the owner
A client can require TLS before login and discard stale capabilities. Count operation classes and tagged outcomes at the owning endpoint.
Visibility and limits
Untagged responses can arrive without a new command. Mailbox names, message literals, credentials and bodies stay outside the routing fixture.
Related catalog hooks
tcp.data tls.client_hello tls.negotiated
POP3 · STLS and implicit TLS
Stack
POP3 over TCP with STLS before authentication or an implicit TLS connection.
Wire messages or local signals
CAPA → STLS → +OK → TLS in authorization state. Later STAT, RETR and QUIT operate in the transaction and update phases.
When events fire
Proposed endpoint triggers include upgrade accepted, authorization completed, message operation completed and session update finished.
Event vocabulary
pop3.command Proposed pop3.reply Proposed pop3.update Proposed tls.negotiated
Objects and lifetimes
A connection advances through authorization, transaction and update. A multiline response belongs to its outstanding command.
Object field examples
pop3.verb, pop3.session_state, pop3.message_number
Actions at the owner
Require the configured transport protection and record only command class and success or failure at the client or server.
Visibility and limits
POP3 calls its upgrade STLS. A positive upgrade reply precedes the handshake. Message bodies and authentication exchanges remain private.
Related catalog hooks
tcp.data tls.client_hello tls.negotiated
SMB 2 and 3
Stack
SMB over direct TCP. SMB over QUIC uses a separate encrypted transport.
Wire messages or local signals
NEGOTIATE → SESSION_SETUP → TREE_CONNECT → CREATE, READ or WRITE → CLOSE. Servers may send lease breaks on an established channel.
When events fire
Proposed endpoint triggers include dialect selected, authenticated session established, share connected, operation completed and lease break received.
Event vocabulary
smb.negotiate Proposed smb.session_ready Proposed smb.request Proposed smb.response Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
A session can use multiple channels. A tree identifies a share and file handles belong to that tree. Message IDs correlate requests and responses.
Object field examples
smb.session_id, smb.tree_id, smb.file_id, smb.message_id
Actions at the owner
An owning client can require signing or encryption and approved server identity. Observe operation counts and status classes per authorized session.
Visibility and limits
Signing authenticates the SMB message. Encryption hides its operations from a packet observer. Share names, paths, principal names and file bytes are private.
Related catalog hooks
tcp.syn tcp.data quic.initial
ONC RPC · service discovery and calls
Stack
ONC RPC over UDP or record-marked TCP. Some services use rpcbind for endpoint discovery.
Wire messages or local signals
rpcbind GETADDR can return a registered endpoint. CALL selects a program, version and procedure. REPLY carries the matching transaction ID.
When events fire
Proposed endpoint triggers include discovery reply validated, call issued, matching reply accepted and timeout reached.
Event vocabulary
rpc.call Proposed rpc.reply Proposed rpc.binding_resolved Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
A registered program maps to an endpoint. The RPC transaction ID correlates a call on its transport. Retransmission can repeat the same call.
Object field examples
rpc.xid, rpc.program, rpc.version, rpc.procedure
Actions at the owner
The client can constrain discovered endpoints to approved services and correlate one reply with its call. Bound pending calls and retry counts.
Visibility and limits
A returned address does not authorize a new VPN destination. RPCSEC_GSS privacy can conceal arguments and results.
Related catalog hooks
udp.open udp.datagram tcp.syn tcp.data
NFS · file access over ONC RPC
Stack
NFSv3 uses ONC RPC, often with separate mount and lock services. NFSv4 performs file operations in COMPOUND calls.
Wire messages or local signals
NFSv3 READ or WRITE returns an RPC result. NFSv4 OPEN, READ and CLOSE can share a COMPOUND. NFSv4.1 sessions use slots on bound connections.
When events fire
Proposed endpoint triggers include export mounted, compound completed, lease or delegation changed and a callback delivered.
Event vocabulary
rpc.call Proposed nfs.operation Proposed rpc.reply Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Mounts reference exports and filehandles. NFSv4 state identifies opens and delegations. A callback or backchannel belongs to the client’s negotiated state.
Object field examples
nfs.version, nfs.file_handle, nfs.compound_index
Actions at the owner
An owning client can pin approved servers, require its selected RPC security flavor, and report operation counts and lease expiration.
Visibility and limits
NFSv3 auxiliary services and NFSv4 callbacks have different transport relationships. A generic inbound grant for any RPC endpoint would exceed either scope.
Related catalog hooks
tcp.data udp.datagram
LDAP · directory operations
Stack
LDAP over TCP with a StartTLS extended operation or TLS established before LDAP.
Wire messages or local signals
StartTLS request → successful extended response → TLS. Bind, Search and Unbind follow the directory session’s authentication state.
When events fire
Proposed endpoint triggers include TLS upgrade accepted, bind outcome, search result entry, final SearchResultDone and session close.
Event vocabulary
ldap.operation Proposed ldap.search_entry Proposed ldap.result Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Message IDs distinguish concurrent operations. A search may produce entries or references before its final result. Connection authentication applies across operations.
Object field examples
ldap.message_id, ldap.operation_kind, ldap.result_code
Actions at the owner
Require the configured TLS identity before a credential-bearing bind. Apply a separate destination policy before following a referral.
Visibility and limits
Referral URLs do not inherit routing authorization. Bind material, directory names, filters and result attributes belong to the directory endpoints.
Related catalog hooks
tcp.data tls.client_hello tls.negotiated
Kerberos · realm and service tickets
Stack
Kerberos AS and TGS exchanges use UDP or TCP to a realm’s KDC. A subsequent application exchange uses the service’s own transport.
Wire messages or local signals
AS-REQ/AS-REP obtains a ticket-granting ticket. TGS-REQ/TGS-REP obtains a service ticket. AP-REQ and optional AP-REP run with the application service.
When events fire
Proposed client triggers include KDC selected, preauthentication requested, ticket acquired, referral realm resolved and service authentication complete.
Event vocabulary
kerberos.request Proposed kerberos.reply Proposed kerberos.service_verified Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Client, realm, KDC and application service are distinct. A ticket and authenticator belong to a principal and service, with explicit lifetimes.
Object field examples
kerberos.realm, kerberos.exchange, kerberos.result
Actions at the owner
Use the configured realm and approved KDC path. At an owning endpoint record outcome classes and expiry without retaining tickets or identities.
Visibility and limits
A ticket exchange and a service socket can reach different destinations. Traffic port, realm text or a referral alone cannot authorize that socket.
Related catalog hooks
udp.datagram tcp.data socket.open
RDP · desktop session
Stack
RDP begins on TCP and negotiates security and channels. Capable peers can add a negotiated UDP multitransport path.
Wire messages or local signals
X.224 connection request/confirm → selected security handshake → channel setup → session traffic. Network Level Authentication can use CredSSP over TLS.
When events fire
Proposed endpoint triggers include security protocol selected, server identity verified, session ready and multitransport channel established or unavailable.
Event vocabulary
rdp.negotiated Proposed rdp.channel_open Proposed rdp.session_ended Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
An RDP session owns its virtual channels and any negotiated UDP transport. The display server remains the server on each approved path.
Object field examples
rdp.selected_protocol, rdp.channel, rdp.session
Actions at the owner
A client can enforce server identity and its minimum security policy. Tie optional transport to the same peer, session and VPN.
Visibility and limits
Encrypted channels hide desktop content, input and credentials. A new UDP tuple needs its own validated association.
Related catalog hooks
tcp.syn tls.client_hello tls.negotiated udp.open
MQTT · brokered messaging
Stack
MQTT 5 over a long-lived TCP connection, optionally protected by TLS. MQTT over WebSocket adds an HTTP handshake and WebSocket framing.
Wire messages or local signals
CONNECT/CONNACK → SUBSCRIBE/SUBACK or PUBLISH. QoS 1 uses PUBACK. QoS 2 uses PUBREC, PUBREL and PUBCOMP. DISCONNECT closes the connection.
When events fire
Proposed endpoint triggers include broker session established, subscription acknowledged, delivery confirmed and keepalive timed out.
Event vocabulary
mqtt.connect Proposed mqtt.publish Proposed mqtt.delivery_completed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
A broker session can survive reconnect according to its expiry policy. Packet identifiers are scoped to the session and direction for the relevant QoS exchange.
Object field examples
mqtt.session, mqtt.qos, mqtt.packet_id
Actions at the owner
The client can require an approved broker and bounded inflight window. Record QoS outcomes and session resumption without retaining topics or payloads.
Visibility and limits
Reconnect can resume a durable session. Repeated messages and dual publisher/subscriber roles prevent inferring application direction from TCP initiation.
Related catalog hooks
tcp.data tls.negotiated http.request
AMQP 1.0 · links and deliveries
Stack
AMQP 1.0 over TCP, optionally with TLS and SASL. A connection multiplexes sessions and links.
Wire messages or local signals
OPEN → BEGIN → ATTACH. FLOW grants link credit. TRANSFER and DISPOSITION track deliveries. DETACH, END and CLOSE tear down each scope.
When events fire
Proposed endpoint triggers include session opened, sender or receiver link attached, credit exhausted, delivery settled and connection closed.
Event vocabulary
amqp.link_attached Proposed amqp.transfer Proposed amqp.delivery_settled Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
A connection contains sessions. Each session has directional sender and receiver links. Deliveries may span transfer frames and be settled later.
Object field examples
amqp.session, amqp.link_handle, amqp.delivery_id
Actions at the owner
An owning endpoint can cap link credit, enforce an approved broker and observe settlement outcomes without recording message addresses or payloads.
Visibility and limits
A TCP client may create both sender and receiver links. AMQP 0-9-1 uses a different wire protocol and method vocabulary.
Related catalog hooks
tcp.syn tcp.data tls.negotiated
SFTP and modern SCP
Stack
TCP → SSH transport → channels → SFTP subsystem
Wire messages or local signals
INIT/VERSION, OPEN, READ, WRITE, CLOSE, STATUS and DATA. Modern OpenSSH scp normally uses SFTP.
When events fire
After subsystem acceptance and version negotiation, emit a complete request on its SSH channel. Match a reply to that channel and request ID. A file handle becomes valid only on a successful OPEN reply.
Event vocabulary
ssh.session sftp.request Proposed sftp.reply Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
SSH connection, authenticated channel, subsystem version, opaque server handle, outstanding request ID and transfer direction.
Object field examples
sftp.channel, sftp.request_id, sftp.handle
Actions at the owner
An owning file service can reject an operation before execution or set transfer quotas. A VPN can route the SSH connection from available endpoint evidence.
Visibility and limits
Several requests can be in flight. Legacy scp uses a different SSH exec protocol. A forwarding SSH tunnel does not expose a nested SSH file session.
Related catalog hooks
ssh.session
TFTP
Stack
UDP → transfer request → newly selected server transfer ID
Wire messages or local signals
Read request, write request, option acknowledgement, DATA, ACK and ERROR.
When events fire
Correlate the first valid server response to the initiating request before binding the transfer ports. Emit block progress once per accepted block. Handle duplicate DATA or ACK as retransmissions.
Event vocabulary
tftp.request Proposed tftp.transfer_bound Proposed tftp.block_accepted Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Client and server transfer IDs, peer addresses, mode, negotiated block size, block progression and timeout belong to one transfer.
Object field examples
tftp.transfer_id, tftp.block, tftp.options
Actions at the owner
An owned server can accept read or write and negotiate options. A connection tracker can consume a bounded expectation for the selected peer and transfer ID.
Visibility and limits
The server chooses a new transfer port. A packet from an arbitrary new endpoint cannot claim an existing transfer. Filenames and file contents should be omitted from default traces.
PostgreSQL and MySQL
Stack
TCP or a local socket → database handshake → optional TLS → database session
Wire messages or local signals
PostgreSQL startup, SSLRequest where used, Parse, Bind, Execute and ReadyForQuery. MySQL server greeting, capability negotiation, COM_QUERY, prepared execution and result packets.
When events fire
Report transport upgrade at the transition to TLS. Emit a statement operation only after parsing the negotiated protocol. Complete a transaction from its protocol-specific status and result sequence.
Event vocabulary
database.session_ready Proposed database.operation Proposed database.result Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Session, authenticated principal reference, prepared statement or portal, transaction status and pending result. Do not use SQL text as a flow key.
Object field examples
database.session, database.transaction, database.operation_kind
Actions at the owner
An owned database gateway can select an authorized backend before session binding or reject a supported operation before execution. Keep later work on its bound transaction.
Visibility and limits
Connection pooling does not make sessions interchangeable during a transaction. An arbitrary SQL query can change state. Authentication exchanges, parameters and row data stay out of default telemetry.
Redis and RESP
Stack
TCP or TLS → RESP framing → client commands and asynchronous pushes
Wire messages or local signals
Command array, ordinary reply, error, subscription delivery and RESP3 push.
When events fire
Emit after the full command frame validates. Track ordinary replies in request order for a pipelined client. Surface asynchronous pushes as a separate operation.
Event vocabulary
redis.command Proposed redis.reply Proposed redis.push Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Connection mode, negotiated RESP version, outstanding command ordinal, subscription and transaction state.
Object field examples
redis.connection, redis.command_name, redis.subscription
Actions at the owner
An owning service can reject commands before execution, apply quotas or route to an authorized upstream before the transaction begins.
Visibility and limits
Pub/sub deliveries can arrive without a pending request. Blocking commands, transactions and pushes prevent naive one-packet/one-reply attribution. Do not trace keys or values by default.
CoAP
Stack
UDP → CoAP, DTLS → CoAP, or a reliable transport with its CoAP framing
Wire messages or local signals
