GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, response codes, ACK and RST. Observe and block-wise transfer extend exchanges.
When events fire
Distinguish a transport acknowledgement from a resource response. Use the token to correlate a delayed response. Emit a logical representation only once all validated blocks are present.
Event vocabulary
coap.request Proposed coap.response_matched Proposed coap.observation_changed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Endpoint, token, message ID where present, observation sequence, resource reference and block context. Reliable transports have different message framing.
Object field examples
coap.token, coap.message_id, coap.resource
Actions at the owner
An owned endpoint can answer a resource request, cap block assembly, or cancel an observation.
Visibility and limits
DTLS or object security such as OSCORE can hide application fields even when transport metadata is available. Do not infer successful application processing from an empty ACK.
IPP printing
Stack
HTTP → optional TLS → IPP message and optional document stream
Wire messages or local signals
Get-Printer-Attributes, Print-Job, Create-Job, Send-Document and Get-Job-Attributes.
When events fire
Emit an IPP operation once the attribute groups are decoded. Track job creation only after a successful reply identifies the job. Document receipt and job completion are separate events.
Event vocabulary
http.request ipp.operation Proposed ipp.job_created Proposed ipp.job_completed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Printer endpoint, request ID, job ID scoped to the printer, document stream and final job state.
Object field examples
ipp.operation_id, ipp.request_id, ipp.printer, ipp.job_id
Actions at the owner
An owned print gateway may reject a request before accepting a document or select an authorized queue. A routing rule may classify the session by known endpoint.
Visibility and limits
Job identifiers are allocated by the printer. Documents, filenames and user-supplied attributes may contain personal information.
Related catalog hooks
http.request http.response

Signaling and media

SIP · transactions and dialogs
Stack
SIP signaling can use UDP, TCP or TLS. SDP offer/answer may appear inside SIP messages. Media travels separately.
Wire messages or local signals
INVITE → provisional response → final response → ACK. BYE ends an established dialog. CANCEL targets a pending INVITE.
When events fire
Existing fixtures cover parsed request and response. Proposed dialog triggers include confirmed branch, renegotiation and orderly release.
Event vocabulary
sip.request sip.response sip.dialog_established Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Transaction identity includes Via branch, method and context. Call-ID and endpoint tags identify a dialog. A forked INVITE can create multiple dialogs.
Object field examples
sip.method, sip.cseq, sip.dialog_id, sip.branch
Actions at the owner
At the signaling owner validate the dialog and peer, scope any media proposal to that branch, and remove pending permissions when it closes.
Visibility and limits
Retransmitted requests and responses are normal. A provisional answer or shared Call-ID alone cannot grant a media path. TLS hides SIP fields in transit.
Related catalog hooks
sip.request sip.response sip.media_offer tls.negotiated
SDP · offer and answer
Stack
SDP describes a proposed session. SIP or another signaling transport carries it. RTP, RTCP, DTLS and ICE use the negotiated media path.
Wire messages or local signals
Offer and answer pair m= media sections with connection addresses, direction attributes, codecs and optional ICE or DTLS parameters.
When events fire
Existing fixture covers a validated media proposal. Proposed owner triggers include answer accepted, stream rejected, direction changed and offer superseded.
Event vocabulary
sip.media_offer sdp.answer Proposed sdp.media_agreed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
A signaling session owns one or more media descriptions. A media identifier correlates negotiated sections. Bundling can share one transport across several media sections.
Object field examples
sdp.media, sdp.transport, sdp.port, sdp.session_version
Actions at the owner
At a signaling endpoint validate both sides and permitted peer sets. Hold a bounded expectation only for the negotiated media and its lifetime.
Visibility and limits
A proposed address or port is untrusted. ICE nomination may select a different candidate pair. SDP bodies can contain credentials and private addresses.
Related catalog hooks
sip.media_offer sip.request sip.response
RTP and RTCP · media and feedback
Stack
RTP transports media and RTCP carries reports or feedback, usually over UDP. Endpoints can negotiate RTP/RTCP multiplexing.
Wire messages or local signals
RTP packets carry sequence number, timestamp and SSRC. RTCP sender and receiver reports describe timing and loss. BYE signals departure.
When events fire
Proposed endpoint triggers include first accepted source, sequence discontinuity, receiver report accepted, source departure and media timeout.
Event vocabulary
rtp.packet Proposed rtcp.report Proposed rtp.source_ended Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
An RTP session can contain several synchronization sources. The negotiated transport, session state and security context scope observations for each SSRC.
Object field examples
rtp.ssrc, rtp.sequence, rtcp.reporter, media.session
Actions at the owner
An owning receiver can validate negotiated payload mappings and report aggregate loss or jitter. Bound source state and age it out on inactivity.
Visibility and limits
An SSRC identifies a synchronization source within a session. RTP and RTCP can share a UDP port. SRTP/SRTCP authentication and encryption constrain which fields a passive observer can trust.
Related catalog hooks
udp.open udp.datagram sip.media_offer
ICE · selecting a media path
Stack
ICE uses signaled candidates, STUN connectivity checks and optional TURN relays. The selected transport can carry DTLS, SRTP and other application data.
Wire messages or local signals
Candidates are exchanged → checks run on candidate pairs → the controlling agent nominates a pair. A restart establishes a new credential generation.
When events fire
Proposed endpoint triggers include pair validated, pair nominated, consent expired, selected pair changed and ICE restarted.
Event vocabulary
ice.pair_checked Proposed ice.pair_selected Proposed ice.consent_expired Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Each ICE transport owns a generation, local and remote candidate sets and a checklist. A nominated pair identifies a path for a specific component.
Object field examples
ice.generation, ice.component, ice.candidate_pair
Actions at the owner
Use only a validated nominated pair and bound consent lifetime. On restart revalidate the new generation before admitting related media.
Visibility and limits
A candidate advertisement or one UDP packet does not prove bidirectional reachability or consent. Candidate credentials and host addresses are private.
Related catalog hooks
udp.open udp.datagram
STUN · binding and consent checks
Stack
STUN transactions often use UDP. ICE uses authenticated Binding requests and responses for connectivity checks and consent freshness.
Wire messages or local signals
Binding request → matching success or error response. XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS reports the requesting endpoint as observed by that server.
When events fire
Proposed endpoint triggers include response matched, integrity verified when required, mapped address changed and transaction timed out.
Event vocabulary
stun.request Proposed stun.response_matched Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
The transaction ID ties a response to its request. An ICE agent additionally scopes the check to its current credentials, generation and candidate pair.
Object field examples
stun.transaction_id, stun.method, stun.mapped_address
Actions at the owner
An owning agent can require the expected responder and integrity protection appropriate to the exchange. Age out unanswered checks.
Visibility and limits
A mapped address describes the server’s observation. Nomination and authorization require separate checks by the ICE agent.
Related catalog hooks
udp.datagram tcp.data
TURN · relayed transports
Stack
A TURN client reaches a relay over its configured transport. A relayed address carries traffic between the allocation and a permitted peer.
Wire messages or local signals
Allocate → CreatePermission → optional ChannelBind → Send/Data indications or ChannelData. Refresh renews or deletes the allocation.
When events fire
Proposed relay or client triggers include allocation created, permission installed, channel bound, allocation refreshed and permission expired.
Event vocabulary
turn.allocation_ready Proposed turn.permission_ready Proposed turn.channel_bound Proposed turn.expired Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
An allocation owns a relayed address and finite lifetime. A TURN permission scopes a peer IP. A channel binding scopes a specific peer transport address.
Object field examples
turn.allocation, turn.peer, turn.channel, turn.expiry
Actions at the owner
At the allocation owner cap permissions, channels and lifetime, and relay only within current grants. Withdraw permission with the owning session.
Visibility and limits
A relay address alone cannot identify the ultimate media peer. Allocation, permission and channel timers are distinct. TURN credentials stay private.
Related catalog hooks
udp.open udp.datagram tcp.data tls.negotiated
WebRTC · DTLS-SRTP and data channels
Stack
ICE selects a path. DTLS-SRTP establishes negotiated SRTP/SRTCP keys for media. WebRTC data channels use SCTP over DTLS.
Wire messages or local signals
ICE nomination → DTLS handshake and fingerprint verification → protected media or data-channel setup. DCEP OPEN/ACK negotiates an in-band data channel.
When events fire
Proposed endpoint triggers include nominated path ready, DTLS fingerprint verified, media keys active, data channel opened and transport closed.
Event vocabulary
ice.pair_selected Proposed dtls.session_ready Proposed media.keys_ready Proposed sctp.message_ready Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
A peer connection owns negotiated transports, media transceivers and data channels. A bundled transport can carry multiple media streams.
Object field examples
ice.generation, dtls.session, media.ssrc, sctp.stream_id
Actions at the owner
At a cooperating endpoint verify the signaled fingerprint, bind media to the selected ICE generation and publish aggregate transport outcomes.
Visibility and limits
DTLS datagrams differ from TLS records on TCP. Packet-only QUIC/TLS hooks cannot decode SRTP, SCTP messages, media or application data here.
Related catalog hooks
udp.open udp.datagram
RTSP
Stack
TCP or protected stream → RTSP → RTP/RTCP over negotiated ports or interleaved channels
Wire messages or local signals
DESCRIBE, SETUP, PLAY, PAUSE, TEARDOWN and matched responses.
When events fire
After successful SETUP, bind the server-selected transport and session to the request. PLAY and TEARDOWN change media state after their own exchanges.
Event vocabulary
rtsp.request Proposed rtsp.reply Proposed rtsp.transport_bound Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Connection, CSeq, session identifier, negotiated media endpoints or interleaved channel IDs, direction and expiry.
Object field examples
rtsp.session, rtsp.cseq, rtsp.transport, rtsp.channel
Actions at the owner
An owned signaling endpoint may admit a bounded media association on a confirmed transport. End it on teardown, loss or expiry.
Visibility and limits
Interleaved RTP stays on the RTSP connection. A separate UDP stream requires its own accepted binding. RTSP resembles HTTP in syntax but has a different state machine.

Operations and routing

Sockets, listeners and app identity
Stack
OS socket or per-app capture → transport flow → VPN member
Wire messages or local signals
Local bind, listen, connect, accept and close. UDP can send to a new peer without connect.
When events fire
On bind or listen, record local intent. At TCP connect or the first UDP send to a destination, evaluate outbound admission. A remote SYN, a completed TCP accept and the first UDP datagram delivered to a socket are three distinct triggers.
Event vocabulary
socket.open socket.listen Proposed socket.accepted Proposed socket.closed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Process evidence belongs to a verified local socket lifetime. A listener can serve many flows. Store local and remote endpoints, transport initiator, member generation and observation source separately.
Object field examples
socket.local_address, socket.remote_address, process.executable_path
Actions at the owner
At a verified outbound admission hook, choose an eligible member. An owned ingress listener may accept or decline an authorized peer. Release bindings when their owner exits.
Visibility and limits
Per-app egress attribution does not identify a remote process. A shared UDP socket may serve many peers. A local flow can start after a remote request, as on the target leg of an SSH reverse forward.
Related catalog hooks
socket.open
Member selection, NAT and related flows
Stack
Inner packet → admitted flow → member transport → peer
Wire messages or local signals
Policy change, first packet, translated return tuple, quoted ICMP error, expectation created or consumed, expiry and member withdrawal.
When events fire
Before a new flow is pinned, evaluate route candidates. Commit the forward and reverse mappings together. On a return, validate the authenticated member and generation. Report a related child only after matching a live expectation.
Event vocabulary
flow.admitted Proposed nat.binding_installed Proposed expectation.consumed Proposed flow.expired Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Keep the pre- and post-translation tuples, initiator role, ingress and egress member, policy revision, parent ID and expiry. Store DNS evidence with its resolver, scope, question and TTL.
Object field examples
flow.member, flow.generation, nat.original_tuple, nat.translated_tuple
Actions at the owner
Select or refuse eligible egress. At an owning translator, apply the pair of mappings and reverse it on return. At an application endpoint, a bounded expectation can propose one child.
Visibility and limits
A fresh inbound request needs service admission. A DNS answer or negotiated port alone grants no service access. The shared WireGuard router currently requires reverse state for incoming service traffic.
Related catalog hooks
ip.packet dns.answer ftp.data_offer sip.media_offer route.advertised route.withdrawn
Split proxy and local replies
Stack
Frontend socket → owned protocol endpoint → backend selection → independent backend socket
Wire messages or local signals
Frontend accept and handshake, target selection, backend dial, application request, response commit and close.
When events fire
After the local endpoint has enough evidence, choose a backend before dialing. A frontend reply may complete a transaction locally. A backend timeout belongs to its own leg and can produce a separate frontend failure.
Event vocabulary
proxy.pre_connect tls.backend_connect proxy.backend_ready Proposed proxy.reply_committed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Two connections have independent tuples, transport state, TLS sessions and timeouts. The request binding links their transactions. Each side keeps its own authentication and verification results.
Object field examples
proxy.frontend, proxy.backend, http.transaction
Actions at the owner
Before commit, an owned endpoint can select an authorized backend, construct a local reply, or build a new request on the other leg.
Visibility and limits
Stream multiplexing can give a single connection many transactions. Retrying a request after its delivery is uncertain needs transaction-specific semantics.
Related catalog hooks
proxy.pre_connect tls.backend_connect http.request http.response
IGMP and MLD
Stack
IPv4 → IGMP or IPv6 → ICMPv6 MLD
Wire messages or local signals
Membership query, report and leave or done. Newer reports include source filters.
When events fire
Emit a membership observation after validating a complete message on the receiving interface. A joined group becomes effective when the owning multicast subsystem confirms it.
Event vocabulary
multicast.report Proposed multicast.membership_changed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Group, source list, include/exclude mode, receiving interface, scope and timer belong to one membership record.
Object field examples
multicast.group, multicast.interface, multicast.sources
Actions at the owner
Observe demand by group. An authorized local multicast endpoint can change its own memberships.
Visibility and limits
Local-link scope and membership timers matter on VPN interfaces. A report from another host does not establish local membership.
Related catalog hooks
ipv4.packet icmpv6.message
BGP
Stack
IP → TCP → BGP session → address family and routes
Wire messages or local signals
OPEN, KEEPALIVE, UPDATE, NOTIFICATION and ROUTE-REFRESH.
When events fire
After session establishment and negotiated capabilities, decode an UPDATE into advertised and withdrawn paths. Report an installed route only when the local routing owner confirms its decision.
Event vocabulary
bgp.update Proposed route.advertised route.withdrawn route.installed Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Peer, routing instance, AFI/SAFI, prefix, next hop, path attributes, optional path ID and generation distinguish candidate paths from selected routes.
Object field examples
bgp.peer, bgp.path_id, route.prefix, route.generation
Actions at the owner
At an owned routing client, filter an import candidate and publish a permitted route to arbitration. A forwarding VPN can only observe eligible lower layers.
Visibility and limits
An UPDATE can carry many routes. Multiple peers can advertise the same prefix. Existing route hooks describe member policy proposals rather than a shipping BGP decoder.
Related catalog hooks
route.advertised route.withdrawn
OSPF and IS-IS
Stack
IP → OSPF or supported link → IS-IS → adjacency and link-state database
Wire messages or local signals
Hello, database exchange, link-state advertisement or PDU, acknowledgement and expiry.
When events fire
Track a neighbor adjacency at the owning router. An accepted newer advertisement changes the database. A completed route computation can then publish an independent route candidate.
Event vocabulary
routing.adjacency_changed Proposed routing.topology_changed Proposed route.advertised
Objects and lifetimes
Routing instance, area or level, interface, router ID, originator, sequence, lifetime and topology revision scope each observation.
Object field examples
routing.instance, routing.area, routing.revision, route.prefix
Actions at the owner
An authorized routing engine can filter exported route candidates at its policy boundary. A monitoring adapter can count topology changes.
Visibility and limits
IS-IS needs a link-capable adapter. A packet tunnel carrying raw IP may see OSPF when the platform actually delivers it. Neither protocol implies an installed host route.
Related catalog hooks
route.advertised route.withdrawn
SNMP and syslog
Stack
SNMP over UDP or a secured transport. Syslog over UDP, TCP or TLS.
Wire messages or local signals
SNMP GET, GETNEXT, GETBULK, SET, RESPONSE, TRAP and INFORM. Syslog sends a structured or legacy message.
When events fire
At an owning manager or agent, emit a complete PDU and correlate confirmed requests with responses. A syslog collector emits a record only after its transport delivers the entire framed message.
Event vocabulary
snmp.request Proposed snmp.response Proposed snmp.notification Proposed syslog.record Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
SNMP uses peer, security context, request ID and variable-binding names. A log event carries facility, severity and the collector’s receipt time. Values and message text can be sensitive.
Object field examples
snmp.request_id, snmp.context, syslog.facility, syslog.severity
Actions at the owner
Count operations, route collection traffic or reject a request before an owned agent commits it. Default traces can retain class and sizes alone.
Visibility and limits
SNMPv3 privacy and syslog over TLS need an authorized endpoint for contents. A trap and a UDP log message have no protocol acknowledgement.
RADIUS
Stack
UDP or protected reliable transport → RADIUS exchange
Wire messages or local signals
Access-Request, Access-Challenge, Access-Accept or Reject, accounting request and response.
When events fire
At an owned authentication client, correlate a response with its pending request and verify its authenticator before publishing a decision. Accounting start/stop are separate observations.
Event vocabulary
radius.request Proposed radius.response_verified Proposed radius.accounting Proposed
Objects and lifetimes
Server identity, client instance, pending identifier, authenticator validation result and retry lifetime scope an exchange. The one-byte identifier alone is insufficient.
Object field examples
radius.code, radius.identifier, radius.client
Actions at the owner
Choose an authorized authentication server before transmission. Count outcomes and latency without logging credentials, shared secrets or complete attributes.
Visibility and limits
A packet claiming Access-Accept has no authority until validated by the endpoint. A routed VPN generally sees only the available transport evidence.

Compiling the same rules for different VPN engines

SimpleVPN owns the grammar, compiler and event VM. The syntax borrows familiar ideas from Rust’s fn and match and Swift’s let and var. F5 iRules and Zeek are closer comparisons for the event model. Swift owns policy validation in the editor and the Network Extension lifecycle. Eligible packet adapters and owned SSH channel hooks run the native Rust evaluator. This page embeds the portable Go reference evaluator as WebAssembly so you can edit policies and trace fixture events offline.

What runs at each proxy boundary

AttachmentProtocol implementationWhere policy and counters apply
Local dynamic SSH listenerApple NIOSOCKS decodes greetings and CONNECT requests on the Mac.The SSH channel hook sees the decoded target and port before opening a channel. The listener preserves initial application bytes sent with the request.
Upstream SOCKS5SagerNet sing encodes CONNECT and UDP ASSOCIATE.gVisor receives the admitted inner packet. TCP opens one upstream stream per flow. UDP keeps its control connection alive and delivers replies for the selected address and port.
HTTP and HTTPS CONNECTGo net/http handles the request and response. HTTPS verifies the proxy certificate and hostname before sending Basic credentials.The packet adapter accounts for inner IP in each direction. Stream counters record relayed bytes. An upstream proxy TLS connection is separate from the application’s TLS session.
Managed remote SSH forwardThe bundled OpenSSH client negotiates the remote listener and delivers channels to private local sockets.ssh.reverse_delivery runs before a local service dial. Admission can deny delivery even after the SSH channel exists.
Owned IPv4 L2TP/IPsecstrongSwan protects UDP/1701 with ESP. lwIP negotiates L2TP and PPP using MSCHAPv2. IPCP supplies the assigned IPv4 address and DNS.Policy sees IPv4 before PPP encapsulation and after authenticated decapsulation. The separate configuration export remains owned by macOS.
Owned IKEv2 and IKEv1strongSwan negotiates IKE and authenticates ESP.Outbound inner policy runs before encryption. Inbound rules see authenticated, decrypted packets before delivery to the Mac.

Following a flow through a proxy member

A shared interface can give WireGuard a private prefix and send other destinations through SOCKS5, HTTP CONNECT or HTTPS CONNECT. This sequence follows a new flow assigned to the proxy. A WireGuard selection instead hands the admitted packet to the member’s WireGuard device for encryption.

In mixed mode the proxy address is numeric. HTTPS needs a certificate valid for that IP address. TCP flows use CONNECT. SOCKS5 can also negotiate UDP ASSOCIATE. A TCP-only proxy carries DNS over TCP and counts other UDP as refused. Reconnect the composition after a physical network change.

Compiler and editor

The macOS event diagram uses a local language server. Select an event to add a handler or jump to an existing one. Source ranges preserve comments and formatting. Numeric edits compile to a register graph that propagates constants and removes unused computations. General handlers bind typed operations to signed Rust routines. Build-time LLVM compilation emits native functions for an exact rule image, with SSA joins, checked arithmetic and bounded loops. A changed image is validated again at activation.

From a saved rule to a packet decision

StageOwnerWhat happens
Build and signRust, XcodeCargo compiles native match routines and the bounded event executor ahead of time. The checker and system extension each link the archive statically.
Edit and validateSwift editor and bundled checkerThe checker targets the selected adapter. Rust compiles compact rules. The Go frontend type-checks rich source against the live packet schema and passes a plan to Rust. The editor requires a versioned success receipt.
ActivateProvider and shared packet routerThe provider independently prepares the native plans before installing the policy. Rejection preserves the previous active plan. An unusable plan cannot select another runtime.
DispatchGo packet adapter and Rust evaluatorThe adapter identifies the event and supplies decoded fields. Compact handlers use indexed candidates. Scalar typed events bind to compiled arithmetic, predicates and edits. The general executor handles network types, table lookups, user functions and bounded loops.
Commit or dropPacket routerRich handlers stage edits across hooks. The router updates counters, applies permitted edits and repairs affected checksums. Missing fields, failed writes and exhausted budgets deny the packet. Compact syntax keeps its declaration-order action semantics.

The signed code is fixed at build time. User policies compile into bounded data before traffic arrives. A simple equality test followed by a constant field write, or a constant prefix test followed by a DSCP mark, can use one precompiled native routine. Compact rules determined entirely by event and port precompute their result. Other typed rules execute a checked instruction plan in Rust. The Go transport still owns packet buffers, connection tracking and VPN egress.

Live packet handler measurements

Median time per validated packet on an Apple M5 Max, across three 240 ms runs of each package benchmark. Both builds used the same packet adapter. The benchmark includes dispatch, field access, edits and counters. Encryption and network I/O are outside the measurement.

Installed rule workloadPortable GoNative Rust path
One compact port count11 ns10 ns
One typed port condition and mark162 ns116 ns
Eight typed port conditions and marks793 ns341 ns
Destination prefix and mark154 ns153 ns
Bounded loop and string conversion447 ns380 ns

The native fixtures recorded zero allocations in the Go heap per dispatch. The Go benchmark does not count allocations made inside Rust. The nearly identical prefix timings fall within the observed run-to-run variation. Reproduce with BenchmarkInstalledRichPacket and BenchmarkEventIndexedDispatch in the packet router test suite, using the release build flags for the native run.

Earlier native code generation experiment

The live router already compiles source into event-indexed bytecode before handling packets. A build-time experiment took one real tcp.syn handler through that compiler, lowered its instructions to C and used Clang to produce native code. Two equivalent source forms checked a port and two IPv4 prefixes, then marked, dropped or continued. One used nested branches and one used short-circuit conditions. Native results matched the Go VM across 16,864 cases. The prototype rejects instructions outside its supported subset.

Measured path on Apple M5 MaxMedian per inputWhat the measurement includes
Go bytecode VM in Go106.5 nsMixed, already-decoded fixture inputs for this rule.
Generated native rule called from C0.99 nsA restricted native lowering of the rule with scalar inputs.
Hand-specialized Swift / Rust called from C0.89 / 0.89 nsEquivalent handwritten native functions with the same C driver.
Hand-specialized Swift / Rust called from Go14.0 / 14.2 nsThe native call plus the Go outbound C ABI crossing for each decoded event.

The fixtures omit packet parsing, TLS, copying real message bodies, VPN encryption, scheduling and network I/O. The existing reusable VM benchmark separately measured about 8.6 ns for a dispatch miss and 167 ns for a matched handler, both at zero heap allocations per iteration. These are specialization measurements on predecoded inputs. The Go VM includes typed host access, diagnostics, accounting and budgeting. End-to-end VPN throughput and application-level Swift or Rust comparisons require measurements in the actual adapters.

Select a tailnet exit node

Open SimpleVPN’s menu bar and choose Exit Nodes to switch a connected standalone Tailscale or Headscale VPN. For per-flow routing, configure each eligible exit node on its own member profile and connect them in a routed composition. Use the stable exit-node ID, available from the menu for an active exit, in the rule. A new flow can select a member already carrying that exit. Existing flows keep their current egress.

Replay an exit-node decision.

Where each provider attaches

Choose Manage VPNs → Set Up a Routed Connection… to put one or more compatible VPNs behind one capture interface. A saved connection can contain up to sixteen members. Each member authenticates separately and supplies its addresses, allowed routes and MTU. The extension checks the configuration before admitting traffic.

flow.profile identifies the saved VPN. Shared rules can also read flow.member and flow.generation for the selected or returning port. A stopped member drops its pinned flows. Credentials stay with each transport. Open the rule or packet inspector to see the totals at the corresponding boundary.

TransportWhere traffic is processed
WireGuard and paired UniFi TeleportThe shared router hands inner IP to the selected WireGuard engine. Its UDP carrier is bound to a physical interface.
OpenVPN, OpenConnect, Tailscale and HeadscaleCompatible authenticated packet drivers hand back addresses and allowed routes. Each member submits and receives its own inner IP through a generation-checked port. All seven OpenConnect families have authenticated packet adapters. Cisco supports its verified transports. Select HTTPS for the other six. Juniper, Pulse and Array require password sign-in, and Array needs its authentication realm.
Built-in IKEv2, Cisco IPsec and L2TP/IPsecA dedicated signed worker owns each security association. L2TP negotiates PPP IPv4. A system configuration exported for use outside the app is managed by macOS.
Proxy Tunnel and SSH Network TunnelThe selected member’s userspace network stack terminates guest TCP. SOCKS5 can also relay UDP. HTTP(S) CONNECT and SSH direct-tcpip can carry DNS over TCP.
Point-to-point SSHAn authenticated tun@openssh.com channel carries complete IPv4 and IPv6 packets. Configure the addresses, remote routes and host-key pin. The server must enable PermitTunnel. A direct point-to-point profile also accepts incoming connections.
SSH local, dynamic and reverse forwardsssh.forward_open checks a fixed local target or SOCKS CONNECT before egress. ssh.reverse_delivery checks a registered incoming channel before it reaches a local service. The private forward sockets verify the connecting process before opening a channel.
OpenConnect with an ocproxy listenerThe supervisor runs the packet rules on both sides of the VPN’s script-tunnel socket. ocproxy owns the local SOCKS service. Its listener is local to that profile.

The optional DNS provider compiles exact names, suffixes and globs when it starts. The Rust matcher selects the first matching resolver rule for each TCP or UDP question. Its activity view reports query, reply and failure counts.

The router installs a compatible capture and resolver policy for the selected group. Per-app capture checks each source against its signed app rules. Negotiated members must agree on resolver addresses and search domains. Independent packet connections retain their own incoming services and negotiated split DNS. routecheck --adapters lists the stable adapter IDs, and --events-for checks a program against that adapter.

Inspect all VPN types and operating modes

One passive FTP transfer, layer by layer

A VPN peer is the FTP client. The laptop is the FTP server. Follow what each observer learns as the control connection progresses. The same command rules work for cleartext FTP and for an endpoint that has decrypted the TLS control stream.

Give a refinement its own hook when the parser recognizes a distinct operation a rule can act on. PASV and EPSV qualify because they initiate passive negotiation. TLS version, encryption state and the location of the listening service are properties of that observation. An upper-layer hook fires when its parser recognizes the operation, even if several packets were needed to assemble it.

TriggerRule eventEvidence available here
Remote client opens the control connectiontcp.synThe packet travels inbound. The destination is the laptop listener. The initiator remains the client throughout the control connection.
The control endpoint completes TLStls.negotiatedThe owner can report the TLS version and its FTP application context. Explicit FTPS upgrades the control connection with AUTH TLS. Implicit FTPS starts with TLS. Data-channel protection has its own negotiation.
A complete PASV or EPSV command arrivesftp.command → ftp.command.passiveOne decoded command drives both subscriptions in order. A drop or evaluation error at the general hook stops the specific hook. The client has requested passive mode. The server has yet to announce a port.
The server returns 227 or 229ftp.replyA parsed 227 carries an address and port. A 229 supplies a port and uses the control connection’s server address. The reply travels outbound from this laptop.
The parser correlates and validates the offerftp.data_offerA rule can request a bounded expectation for a later data connection. The passive client opens that connection toward the server. Active FTP reverses the data connection’s initiator.

On the shared router, an outbound TCP payload can fire ip.packet, ipv4.packet or ipv6.packet, tcp.data, then tls.client_hello when the parser finds a complete visible name. An owned FTP command can read ip.server_address, ftp.command and, when supplied by its TLS endpoint, tls.version. Missing evidence raises an evaluation error if a handler reads it. Each parser needs its own evidence. A packet can contain part of a TLS record, and one decrypted record can contain several FTP commands. A forwarding router can observe TCP and a visible ClientHello. Decoded FTP requires cleartext or a cooperating TLS endpoint. The playground accepts already-parsed observations and dispatches command specializations from their verbs.

For an existing ftps.handshake rule, the interpreter retains an FTP-scoped compatibility handler. New rules can use tls.negotiated with tls.application_protocol for the handshake and ftp.command for each decoded command.

Whole-system event map

Trace an event inside its state machine, then follow a dashed arrow to the exact state in another machine. Dotted links connect comparable observations across the legacy and simulator views without implying a call or a time order.

Drag to pan. Use the zoom buttons or pinch to read labels. With the map focused, use arrow keys to pan, + or − to zoom, and Home to fit. Selecting a transition shows its direction and evidence below.

All machines

Native routing control plane

Host routing control plane

Swift mediators arbitrate route, DNS and proxy settings. These transitions run in the app and packet tunnel extension. The control surface separately publishes status, gateway, profiles and denied notifications to subscribers.

Submit or update intent
Watching → Intent captured

A route, DNS or proxy mediator receives the current intent for one engine. The capture callback can retain the pushed values for inspection.

Run intentHook
Intent captured → Effective intents

The profile’s filter rewrites the captured intent before arbitration. An absent filter passes the intent through.

Withdraw engine
Watching → Effective intents

Disconnect or withdrawal removes the engine’s entry.

Arbitrate
Effective intents → Plan ready

The arbiter computes one plan from the participating engines and current policy.

Change owner or preferences
Watching → Plan ready

A policy change can trigger arbitration over existing intents.

Plan already applied
Plan ready → Watching

An unchanged plan can reuse the last successful result.

Queue latest plan
Plan ready → Applying

The apply loop serializes realization and coalesces pending changes.

New plan while busy
Applying → Applying

The in-flight operation completes before the latest pending plan is realized.

Apply completed
Applying → Watching

The realizer reports completion. The applied state provides the baseline for later changes.

Apply rejected
Applying → Apply error

Validation, network settings or a provider acknowledgement can fail. The operation reports the error.

Reconcile again
Apply error → Plan ready

A later policy or connection change can produce a fresh plan.

Observe host change
Watching → Drift candidate

The route socket observes default-route changes. System Configuration observes DNS and proxy state.

Expected or suppressed
Drift candidate → Watching

A change that agrees with the plan, or is suppressed as a recent self-write, needs no correction.

External difference
Drift candidate → Drift confirmed

A confirmed change produces a drift event at the owning mediator.

Publish observation
Drift confirmed → Watching

The UI can surface the observed difference.

Reassert desired state
Drift confirmed → Applying

When the mediator chooses to restore the intended configuration it asks the realizer to apply it again.

Validate virtual policy
Applying → Candidate checked

On the shared virtual router path, validate the candidate revision, member configuration and Network Extension settings.

Network settings accepted
Candidate checked → Host configured

The packet tunnel provider completes the macOS network settings update.

Network settings rejected
Candidate checked → Apply error

The provider reports failure before committing the router policy.

VRApplyPolicy succeeds
Host configured → Watching

The extension commits the policy, publishes the new revision and acknowledges the request.

VRApplyPolicy fails
Host configured → Tunnel cancelled

A router commit failure after host configuration cancels the tunnel and returns an error.

Routing layers

macOS can give an inner IP packet to a VPN, deliver a query to the DNS extension, or run a system VPN itself. The configured adapter determines who can inspect the traffic and where a rule can run.

Processing boundaries

Configuration and status

Owner · SimpleVPN controller, engine callbacks and macOS

The app installs eligible profiles, routes, DNS settings and proxy preferences. Reported status, assigned addresses and advertised routes return to the controller. An advertised prefix is a control-plane proposal; the selected member and its peer permissions still govern each new flow.

Show entries at this layer
Socket and process

Owner · Originating app, macOS source attribution, verified identity service

A TCP connect, UDP connect or first UDP send to a destination supplies the socket.open fixture. Stored signed-app criteria and temporary process instances apply in the live per-app WireGuard configuration. macOS attribution reaches the provider with a captured packet. A configured identity verifier can check the signing requirement and process conditions there.

Show entries at this layer
Capture boundary

Owner · macOS Network Extension and the selected packet tunnel

macOS directs whole-Mac routes or eligible per-app traffic into an NE packet flow. Delivery starts at the inner IPv4 or IPv6 header. Raw packets from separately configured tunnel engines go to their own adapters. Socket allocation, local binding and DNS resolution alone do not create an admitted VPN flow.

Show entries at this layer
Shared flow router

Owner · Virtual WireGuard composition · packetrouter

The router validates the capture source and tuple. For a new flow it selects the most-specific source override, source default, destination claim or configured default, as applicable. A selected port must be active, have the right address family and permit the destination. It pins the winning member, generation and translated tuple. The typed or legacy outbound policy runs before forwarding.

Show entries at this layer
Inner IP and ICMP

Owner · Outbound packet parser and event VM

Eligible outbound packets enter ip.packet and then their IPv4 or IPv6 hook. ICMP and ICMPv6 expose validated message fields. DSCP edits preserve ECN. The router owns validation, translation, MTU handling and checksum updates.

Show entries at this layer
TCP and UDP

Owner · Outbound packet parser and per-flow state

A SYN with ACK clear can trigger tcp.syn, including a retransmission. TCP payload is eligible for tcp.data. UDP invokes udp.open for a new binding and udp.datagram for eligible outbound datagrams. Ports on the wire and endpoint roles carry different meanings. An owned UDP fixture can rebuild an entire datagram.

Show entries at this layer
Protocol evidence

Owner · Packet parser, optional flow inspector and endpoint-specific decoders

A validated UDP question to port 53 can trigger dns.query. A matching reply can supply a scoped DNS association until expiry. The packet hook can inspect a complete visible ClientHello in one TCP payload or a public QUIC Initial header. The optional inspector can accumulate bounded TCP handshake evidence. Encrypted application data and concealed names require evidence from a cooperating endpoint.

Show entries at this layer
Authenticated return

Owner · WireGuard member and reverse flow table

The tunnel engine decrypts the outer transport first. The router looks up the inner reverse tuple together with the receiving member and generation, restores the original capture destination, and writes the packet to macOS. Unmatched returns drop. Related ICMP errors require their own validated quoted-flow match. Reply evidence and counters can update here.

Show entries at this layer
WireGuard encapsulation

Owner · App-owned WireGuard peer engine

The selected member receives a translated inner IP packet, checks its peer configuration and sends protected traffic to the peer. On return, its tunnel engine authenticates and decrypts outer datagrams before delivering inner IP to the shared router. Peer handshake and byte counters belong to engine status.

Show entries at this layer
Outer network

Owner · VPN transport, macOS IP stack and physical network

Outer endpoints identify tunnel peers or proxy servers. The wire carries the tunnel’s own data and control traffic. Multiple client IP flows can share one protected transport. Link-layer or outer headers do not identify the original application’s plaintext.

Show entries at this layer
Client-facing proxy

Owner · Local TCP stack or trusted terminating frontend

A locally accepted TCP session has a client-side handshake, endpoint and lifetime. The shipped Proxy Tunnel can require a visible TLS ClientHello and choose a configured backend, then relay the original bytes. Plaintext HTTP, FTP, SIP or decrypted TLS/QUIC handlers in the playground require a separately modeled protocol endpoint.

Show entries at this layer
Backend connection

Owner · Owned proxy dialer, upstream proxy or SSH session

The dialer opens a separate connection or channel toward the backend. The configured upstream may negotiate SOCKS5, HTTP CONNECT or HTTPS CONNECT, or open an SSH forwarding channel. A terminating TLS fixture creates a fresh backend handshake with an independently verified peer and upstream SNI. A frontend reply and a backend reply go to different peers.

Show entries at this layer
Owned protocol endpoint

Owner · Protocol parser and related-session owner

After authorized termination or cleartext parsing, HTTP messages, FTP commands and SDP offers have application meaning. A trusted FTP or SIP endpoint may model one bounded child-flow expectation. The data or media flow needs its own tuple, direction and member authorization. Nested encryption limits visibility on either leg.

Show entries at this layer
Independent tunnel engines

Owner · App-owned OpenVPN 3, OpenConnect, Tailscale, WireGuard and SSH adapters

Standalone VPN packet pumps hand inner IP to their selected core. Each core owns its session, encryption, negotiated routes and data transport. Tailscale and Headscale use the same local node. The SSH Network Tunnel owns its netstack and channels; external SSH helper modes expose process lifecycle. These adapters do not install a live general-purpose rich packet program.

Show entries at this layer
System VPN

Owner · macOS personal VPN and IPsec stack

SimpleVPN observes the status of its native IKEv2 and Cisco IPsec sessions. An exported L2TP profile has a separate external owner. SimpleVPN can configure them and observe reported status. macOS owns negotiation, security associations, encapsulation and the packet path. The ipsec.sa fixture needs an explicitly controlled endpoint to provide its observations.

Show entries at this layer
DNS query proxy

Owner · Dedicated DNS proxy system-extension provider

When enabled, the DNS extension accepts eligible UDP DNS proxy flows from macOS and sends each question to the resolver selected by its own rule or default. Resolver activity counts belong to that extension. A later application connection has its own source and route selection.

Show entries at this layer
Ethernet and VLAN

Owner · Link-aware fixture adapter

The optional link fixture starts with an Ethernet frame and can decode an 802.1Q tag. A Mac packet-tunnel delivery begins at an IP header. The physical interface may use its own link framing outside the VPN.

Show entries at this layer

Events and objects by layer

Typed events open their state diagrams. Legacy hooks use the compact rule language. The session simulator can dispatch two hooks on one packet, such as udp.open + dns.query or udp.open + quic.initial. Each hook appears under its own name below.

A server on the laptop

A remote client can send the first SYN or datagram. The laptop then owns the listening socket and sends the service reply. Compare that exchange with a reply to a connection the laptop started.

The shared WireGuard router admits replies through an existing reverse mapping scoped to the VPN member and its generation. A new remote request to the laptop has no such mapping and is dropped. Standalone WireGuard can deliver authenticated incoming IP to macOS. A listening service, host firewall policy and return route determine whether a client can use it.

      Event lifecycle
      

      Choose a machine and follow a transition to see which event can fire next. Jump to a typed event to inspect its trigger, direction and example.
      

      Live typed packet runs in the outbound WireGuard composition router. Observed in app identifies evidence from a shipping engine or inspector. The general typed handler for that observation runs in the lab. Typed fixture takes its evidence from the offline example.
      

      



      


      

      Socket admission
      

      The socket fixture makes one decision for a new outbound destination. In a live per-app WireGuard session macOS delivers an attributed packet later. Its audit token enters a separate signed-process verifier.

      All transitions in this machine (5)
      Socket allocatedLocal · State change
      No destination → No destination
      Allocation or a local bind leaves the remote endpoint unknown.
      socket.openClient → remote · Typed fixture
      No destination → Policy evaluating
      TCP connect, UDP connect or the first UDP send-to for a new destination supplies transport, family and a remote address and port. The fixture can also carry local endpoints, signer evidence, executable and ancestor paths, and a named proxy comparison.
      Policy selects a memberLocal · State change
      Policy evaluating → Member selected
      A rule can call source.select_member after checking its evidence. A verified signer alone cannot establish an ancestor or proxy condition.
      Drop or evaluation errorLocal · State change
      Policy evaluating → Denied
      A drop stops the event. Reading an unavailable field, failing a lookup key evaluation or exceeding a runtime limit discards staged effects.
      Flow closesEither direction · State change

      Routing object and function reference
      

      Start with the event your handler receives. For example, socket.open exposes the connecting process, while tcp.syn exposes the outbound handshake. Expand a field’s event scopes to see where it can be read or changed, then select an event to replay it.
      

      Types, access and missing evidence
      bool
      true or false. A missing observation fails when read.
      int
      Signed 64-bit integer. JSON replay input and output must fit the exactly representable range −(2⁵³−1) through 2⁵³−1.
      string
      Valid UTF-8, up to 4,096 bytes. Comparisons preserve case.
      addr
      A numeric IPv4 or IPv6 address without a scope or mapped IPv4 representation.
      prefix
      An aligned IP network and its CIDR prefix length.
      dns
      A normalized ASCII DNS name. Use dns() to construct one.
      bytes
      Opaque octets, up to 65,535. Replay input uses JSON arrays of 0–255, up to 8,192 bytes per value.
      []T
      An array of up to 64 elements of one scalar type T. Indices start at zero.
      Reading an unavailable field fails the event. A supplied zero, empty value or false remains a value. The compiler checks field names, argument counts, argument types and write access for the named event. The host validates each proposed edit. A failed or dropped replay restores the original fields and clears staged actions.
      “Outbound packet hook and replay” means the packet adapter exposes this field to live outbound handlers. Other entries are available for typed replay. A protocol engine can report observations without exposing a live programmable handler. Each event link identifies its observation boundary. Binary work, loops and execution are bounded. Source functions declare typed arguments and a return type, for example fn clamp(n: int) -> int { if n > 1200 { return 1200; } return n; }.

      Functions and actions
      Binary data 6
      bytes(hex: string) → bytes
      Decode pairs of hexadecimal digits. Each pair supplies one octet. Whitespace, an odd length and non-hexadecimal digits fail.
      let payload = bytes("01af");
      Pure expression. Available in functions and event handlers.
      byte(data: bytes, index: int) → int
      Read one unsigned octet, 0–255, at a zero-based byte offset. A negative index or an offset outside the buffer fails.
      let version = byte(bytes("01af"), 0);
      Pure expression. Available in functions and event handlers.
      u16be(data: bytes, offset: int) → int
      Read two consecutive bytes as one unsigned big-endian integer, 0–65535. Both bytes must fit at a nonnegative offset.
      let portNumber = u16be(bytes("01bb"), 0);
      Pure expression. Available in functions and event handlers.
      write_u16be(data: bytes, offset: int, value: int) → bytes
      Return a copy with an unsigned 16-bit value written most significant byte first. Both target bytes must fit and the value must be 0–65535.
      let edited = write_u16be(bytes("000000"), 1, 443);
      Pure expression. Available in functions and event handlers.
      slice(data: bytes, start: int, end: int) → bytes
      Return bytes from start inclusive to end exclusive. Require 0 ≤ start ≤ end ≤ byte length. Equal bounds produce an empty value.
      let head = slice(bytes("010203"), 0, 2);
      Pure expression. Available in functions and event handlers.
      replace(data: bytes, start: int, end: int, replacement: bytes) → bytes
      Return a copy with [start, end) replaced. Equal bounds insert and empty replacement deletes. Bounds must be ordered and in range. Results over 65,535 octets fail.
      let edited = replace(bytes("01ff03"), 1, 2, bytes("02"));
      Pure expression. Available in functions and event handlers.
      Collections 3
      len(value: string | dns | bytes | []T) → int
      Count UTF-8 octets in text or DNS values, octets in bytes, or elements in arrays. Integers and addresses require an explicit conversion before measuring their rendered form.

      Pure expression. Available in functions and event handlers.
      range(start: int, end: int) → []int
      Return ascending integers from start inclusive to end exclusive. Equal bounds return an empty array. Reversed bounds and more than 64 elements fail.

      Pure expression. Available in functions and event handlers.
      at(values: []T, index: int) → T · at(data: bytes, index: int) → int

    missing { drop(); }

      Test for an exact, case-sensitive suffix. An empty suffix matches. Use a leading dot when the suffix must begin at a DNS label boundary.
      let internal = ends_with(dns("api.office.example"), ".office.example");
      Pure expression. Available in functions and event handlers.
      



      Typed language reference
      Writing a handler
      

      The playground runs the Go compiler and bytecode evaluator embedded as WebAssembly. The host is a local fixture. A field edit changes the decoded fixture and an action records the operation an adapter would perform. The simulator below models how a sequence of those operations affects connections.
      

      

      Events, objects and assignment
      on office: tcp.syn {
  if ip.server_address in prefix("10.0.0.0/8") {
    ip.dscp = 18;
  }
}
      A handler has a unique name and subscribes to an event. Dotted fields belong to objects such as ip, tcp, dns and tls. Each event publishes its own typed field set. Use the searchable reference in the playground to see which fields are readable or writable. Reads of absent fixture evidence report an error.
      

      Match the process that opened a connection
      on terminal_curl: socket.open runs when an outbound socket first acquires a destination. terminal_curl names the rule. TCP connect, UDP connect or the first UDP send to a new peer provides the trigger. The same process can open multiple flows, each with its own decision. The socket carries the actual peer address and port. Its process context identifies the caller.
      In the curl playbook, the executable path is /usr/bin/curl. The ancestor chain contains both the interactive shell and Terminal’s executable. A new curl invocation can match the same rule with a different PID. A PID plus its kernel generation lets the helper verify which instance supplied evidence.
      The native source rule begins with a verified signed executable and checks its configured name, location, ancestor and proxy variable. For a signed launcher app such as Terminal, macOS can narrow capture using a launcher rule with the signed tool in matchTools. The packet still needs an attributable source to pass the helper’s checks. For a proxy check, the helper compares a specific credential-free host and port. The rule receives a verdict. An unavailable identity or restricted launch environment cannot authorize the connection. A controlled launch of Apple’s /usr/bin/curl on the development Mac produced the unavailable outcome. The fourth event reproduces this case. macOS may attribute a socket to a responsible app, and that attribution alone cannot prove which child opened it.
      HTTP_PROXY and http_proxy are separate, case-sensitive choices. curl itself uses lowercase http_proxy for HTTP. The uppercase example matches a launch condition. Setting it does not establish that curl connected through that proxy. For the actual destination, inspect the connection’s remote address and port.
      The socket.open playbook supplies decoded evidence as fixtures. The live helper returns the matching source-rule ID to the packet router. The VM can match that ID via flow.source.
      

      Variables, functions and loops
      fn is_web(port: int) -> bool {
  for candidate in [443, 8443] {
    if candidate == port { return true; }
  }
  return false;
}

on classify: tcp.syn {
  let web = is_web(port.server);
  if web { ip.dscp = 18; } else { count(); }
}
      Declare locals with let, assign with = and return a typed value with return. Conditions require booleans. for … in iterates a bounded array or range. Pass event fields as arguments. Functions operate on their parameters and immutable tables, and must return a value on every path.
      

      Network types and conversion
      bool, int, string, bytes, addr, prefix and dns keep incompatible values distinct. addr("2001:db8::1") parses an address. prefix("2001:db8::/32") parses a network. dns("Lab.Example.") normalizes a DNS name. string(value) produces a representation for text operations.
      Use address in network for membership and mask(address, bits) to derive a network. ==, !=, numeric comparisons, arithmetic and boolean operators build expressions. TLS fields describe a particular handshake leg. Read tls.sni where a visible client name exists and edit the upstream name on a separate backend-handshake event.
      

      Tables and external data
      table networks: prefix -> int = external "sites";
on classify: ip.packet {
  match lookup(networks, ip.dst) {
    found(class) { ip.dscp = class; }
    missing { count(); }
  }
}
      A table lookup has two outcomes, found(value) or missing. The compiler requires both arms. Only the found arm binds a value of the table’s element type. An empty string, zero, false or an empty byte buffer can be present. An invalid key expression or unavailable evidence raises an evaluation error before either arm runs. An address looked up in a prefix table uses longest-prefix match. Other key types use exact lookup. The playground’s table editor and local JSON importer both use the following shape.
      {"sites":{"key":"prefix","element":"int",
  "entries":[{"key":"10.0.0.0/8","value":18}]}}
      A missing external data set or invalid row is a compile error. The compiler validates and indexes the table before replay. Changing the JSON compiles a new snapshot. A handler performs no file or network access while it runs.
      

      Header and content access
      Writable fields belong to the boundary that can rebuild them. The inner IP adapter can mark DSCP, the TCP adapter can clamp an existing MSS, and an owned UDP fixture can expose a byte buffer. Byte operations use checked offsets. A bounds or type error discards the event’s staged edits. No packet or certificate leaves this document.
      Handlers own field assignments and actions. A helper can return the value for a handler to assign. An Ethernet frame can expose a link address that a macOS layer-3 tunnel never received. An SSH channel can expose a destination even when the underlying application data is encrypted.
      

      Follow the result
      Step executes one more fixture event, Back reconstructs the preceding state, and Run all evaluates the entire sequence. Check branch line numbers against the editor. A handler entry counts whenever its event fires. A false condition can produce an entry with no field change. The before/after table shows exactly what changed.
      Use the stateful simulator to see separate client and server legs, temporary FTP expectations, and DNS history. Its fixtures distinguish a cleartext or authorized terminating endpoint from encrypted passthrough. The IP route tester below evaluates the smaller policy 1 language.
      

      Standard library
      addr, prefix, dns, int, string and bytes convert typed values. bytes("0010") decodes hexadecimal. lower, contains, starts_with and ends_with work on text. len measures a string, byte buffer or array. at indexes a byte buffer or array.
      byte(data, offset) and u16be(data, offset) read bytes and network-order integers. slice, replace and write_u16be return an edited buffer to assign back to a writable field. range(start, end) builds a bounded sequence. match lookup(table, key) distinguishes presence from absence and mask masks an address to a prefix.
      Execution boundaries
      The editor compiles the source to typed instructions. Event dispatch skips handlers attached to other events. Literal data stays in the program, and lookup tables are indexed before evaluating traffic. The live routing path uses the adapter’s supported subset. Inspection in this file uses the larger fixture schema.
      Packet ownership matters. A parsed DNS question can expose a name and recursion flag. A SIP or FTP endpoint can describe a proposed related flow. A program can issue a local reply only on an event with a local endpoint. A certificate and its private key are never inputs to these fixtures.
      Syntax at a glance
      At the top level declare fn, table or on. Within a block, let x: int = 1; and var x = 1; introduce a typed local. Use x = x + 1; to update it. End simple statements with a semicolon. Use braces for if, else if, else and for. Both # and // introduce line comments. Double quotes enclose text.
      Operators from low to high precedence are ||, &&, equality and in, comparisons, + -, * / %, then unary ! -. Group expressions with parentheses. Index arrays or bytes using items[0]. Offsets are zero-based, and range and slice end positions are exclusive.
      

      Inline data and limits
      table names: int -> string = {
  443: "web", 8443: "alternate"
};
on service: tcp.syn {
  match lookup(names, port.server) {
    found(label) { count(); }
    missing { drop(); }
  }
}
      A table can contain up to 4,096 distinct keys. The browser’s JSON importer accepts up to 32 external tables with 2,048 rows each. Each program can declare 64 tables with 16,384 entries in total. Each array holds up to 64 values of one type. A program can declare up to 128 handlers and 128 functions in 64 KiB of source. Recursive calls are rejected. The VM limits each event to 8,192 instructions and budgets work on variable-length data. A runtime error identifies the event and discards staged changes.

      Language reference
      Routing rules and event handlers
      

      Build 541 uses the WireGuard composition editor for live IP and source routing. The checkout adds compiled packet-event handlers and inspection. Operations prefixed with sim. below describe the full-proxy model in this file. The simulator works on decoded fixture events.
      

      

      Destination and source rules
      policy 1
rule finance app signed browser ip 10.42.8.19 via lab
rule browse app signed browser via work
rule build process build-job via lab
default drop
      The offline routecheck language also accepts rule ID ip ADDRESS[/PREFIX] via MEMBER. A rule action is via MEMBER or drop. Use canonical IPv4 or IPv6 networks. Put specific matches first. Each source needs a catchall and a source policy ends in default drop. A destination-only policy may use default via MEMBER.
      The live composition binds actual member IDs and verified app or process identities. The host override takes priority over that source’s default. macOS capture and WireGuard Allowed IPs still apply.
      

      Attach code to an event
      on ID EVENT [FIELD VALUE ...] => ACTION [ARG]
on web tcp.syn port 443 => clamp-mss 1280
on calls udp.open dst 10.0.0.0/8 => mark-dscp 46
on lab dns.query name lab.example => count
      One handler per line. # starts a comment. IDs begin with an ASCII letter and can contain letters, digits, hyphens and underscores. Predicates on a line are combined with AND. Handlers for the same event execute in declaration order, including wildcard and port-specific handlers. A drop stops that packet.
      The native compiler checks operands, action/event compatibility and CIDR boundaries once. It builds dispatch tables by event and destination port. Blank configurations bypass handler dispatch. The native limit is 128 handlers and 32 KiB.
      

      Fields and actions
      port matches the destination port. dst matches an IP or canonical network. source matches a verified source rule ID. name matches an exact DNS question or visible TLS server name, ignoring case. A DNS lookup and an SNI observation remain separate evidence.
      count records a match. drop discards the matching packet. mark-dscp 0…63 changes the inner IP traffic class and preserves ECN. clamp-mss 536…65535 lowers an existing TCP SYN MSS option. set-dns-rd 0|1 changes the recursion-desired flag on a recognized UDP DNS question. The router repairs affected checksums.
      

      When each packet hook fires
      tcp.syn sees outbound opening SYNs, including retransmissions. udp.open sees the first datagram of a new tracked tuple. dns.query sees a parsed cleartext question to UDP port 53. quic.initial recognizes the public long-header shape of a v1 or v2 Initial datagram. Protected QUIC contents remain opaque to this hook.
      tls.hello in the packet hook requires a complete parseable ClientHello with a visible SNI in the packet. The observational inspector can separately assemble a bounded prefix across segments. Split records, ECH, or a missing SNI can leave the packet hook without a match. An allowlist requiring a backend decision before first egress belongs at the proxy boundary.
      

      Two independent connections
      In the split-proxy simulation the client receives a local handshake response. The backend packet count can remain zero while the proxy waits for a ClientHello. Once enough evidence exists, a named rule commits an approved backend. An unknown name can receive a local rejection with no backend dial.
      Passing through a TLS ClientHello preserves its original bytes. Completing TLS locally requires an identity the client trusts. To change upstream SNI or TLS parameters, the proxy creates and verifies a separate upstream TLS session. Client certificate pinning, mutual TLS and ECH can limit what it can terminate.
      

      DNS and related sessions
      A DNS observation has a resolver, scope and expiry. A flow to an answer IP can have several candidate hostnames. A shared IP alone cannot prove the requested name. The simulator shows which evidence an event actually supplies.
      A passive FTP response announces a server-side data port. An active FTP command announces a client-side port. Model the data connection as a child of the control connection, constrained by direction, peer addresses, port, VPN and expiry. Consume an expectation once. A late or mismatched connection cannot claim it. For FTPS, access to commands inside TLS depends on authorized termination of the control channel.
      

      Full-proxy operations in the simulator
      sim.client.hello can select a backend or set upstream-sni for a new upstream handshake. sim.client.request and sim.server.reply can produce a local reply-client or reply-server. These operations apply to the named side of the simulated proxy.
      sim.ftp.active and sim.ftp.passive can create a timed expect-data entry. sim.quic.hello represents a name supplied by an authorized QUIC endpoint. A protected Initial by itself cannot supply that event. Choose a preset to see executable examples.
      

      Reading counters and state
      A packet may increment multiple handler counters before its routing rule selects a VPN. Adding them together double-counts traffic. Rule counters in the native inspector cover matched packet bytes, outgoing and return traffic where applicable, and drops. The connection table shows the original and translated addresses, ports, member generation and observed names.
      Missing evidence is shown as unknown. A temporary process identity includes its generation. A traffic graph is a series of counter deltas. In the simulator each x-axis position is a fixture event. Rewinding reconstructs the counters, connections and expectations at that point.

      3. Packet tunnel extensiongVisor netstackTCP → SOCKS CONNECTBuilds IP packets
      4. Proxy serverSOCKS5 proxyOpens target socketRelays target bytes
      5. Remote networkTarget serviceTCP destinationSends reply
      

       Selected path
      

      Return path
      The proxy relays target bytes back to the extension. Its netstack builds local reply packets. A successful UDP association returns datagrams through the granted relay.
      

      Local processing
      The proxy tunnel reads IP packets and terminates guest TCP in its userspace netstack. It connects to the upstream proxy and requests the destination host and port.
      UDP
      For UDP, it requests SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE and sends datagrams through the granted relay. If unavailable, ordinary UDP fails. DNS can retry over TCP.
      Transport privacy
      SOCKS5 supplies forwarding. The bare SOCKS5 hop supplies no transport encryption of its own. Application TLS, when used, still protects application data.
      Packet and event sequence
      Read the Stevens diagram from top to bottom. Arrows show messages on the example path. Dots show local decisions. Time is schematic.
      

      CONNECT asks the proxy to open a TCP tunnel
      HTTP CONNECT and HTTPS CONNECT use the same target-selection mechanism. HTTPS adds TLS between the Mac and the proxy.
      

       OutboundReturn pathTCP byte stream
      1. User processAny appApplication socketReply to socket
      2. macOSVirtual interfaceRouted destinationsDelivers reply
      3. Packet tunnel extensionProxy tunnelSends CONNECTRebuilds guest TCP
      4. Proxy serverHTTP(S) proxyDials host and portRelays target bytes
      5. Remote networkTarget serviceTCP destinationSends reply
      

       Selected path
      

      Return path
      Target bytes come back through the established CONNECT tunnel. The extension netstack reconstructs TCP/IP packets and macOS delivers them to the originating app.
      

      Handshake
      The extension terminates guest TCP and requests a tunnel to the destination. With HTTPS CONNECT it establishes TLS to the proxy before sending the CONNECT request.
      Bytes
      After acceptance, the proxy relays the byte stream. An app’s HTTPS session can run end to end inside it. HTTP CONNECT alone provides no encryption on the proxy hop.
      Protocol limits
      These upstreams carry TCP. SimpleVPN handles UDP DNS on port 53 using DNS over TCP and refuses other UDP.
      Packet and event sequence
      Read the Stevens diagram from top to bottom. Arrows show messages on the example path. Dots show local decisions. Time is schematic.
      

      The application can choose a proxy before it opens a socket
      A proxy-aware app consults macOS settings. A manual endpoint, exception list or PAC decision can change the socket’s actual destination.
      

       OutboundReturn pathTCP byte stream
      1. User processProxy-aware appReads system settingsReads response
      2. User processProxy decisionManual or PACPrior proxy choice
      3. macOSRoute lookupRoute to chosen proxyExisting connection
      4. Proxy serverSelected proxyForwards requestRelays response
      5. Remote networkTarget serviceRequested endpointSends response
      

       Selected path
      

      Return path
      The target response returns through the chosen proxy connection. Any tunnel carrying that socket handles its own independent return path.
      

      Order matters
      A PAC script can select a proxy or DIRECT for a URL. Here the result selects a proxy. DIRECT skips the proxy and still follows normal IP routing.
      Multiple VPNs
      The proxy connection itself follows the applicable macOS routes. A selected VPN can carry that connection. A physical route can also carry it.
      Local endpoints
      A system SOCKS endpoint can point to the SSH dynamic listener. Apps that ignore system proxy settings open their own sockets and follow normal IP routing.

      A subprocess SSL VPN can expose a local SOCKS endpoint
      Certain OpenConnect profile options select the external tool path. SimpleVPN then uses ocproxy to expose the remote VPN network to proxy-aware clients.

      3. On this MacOpenConnect toolCarries VPN trafficReads VPN traffic

       Selected path
      

      Return path
      The gateway returns traffic over OpenConnect. ocproxy relays the resulting bytes back to the app’s local SOCKS connection.
      

      Selection
      The ordinary in-process OpenConnect path can carry routed IP packets. This scenario is the subprocess configuration that starts openconnect with ocproxy.
      Traffic scope
      The application explicitly uses the local proxy, or honors a system SOCKS setting pointing to it. The subprocess path exposes no whole-Mac VPN interface.
      Placement
      The local SOCKS endpoint and external client run on this Mac. OpenConnect carries traffic over the VPN to the remote gateway.

      A name rule chooses the resolver for a lookup
      With query routing enabled, the DNS proxy inspects an eligible question such as api.lab.example and sends it to the configured resolver.
      

       OutboundReturn pathDNS question and reply
      1. User processApplicationRequests an addressReceives answer
      2. macOSResolverIssues DNS questionDelivers DNS answer
      3. DNS proxy extensionQuery matcherExact, suffix or globValidates response
      4. macOSNetwork pathRoute to resolver IPResolver connection
      5. Resolver hostDNS serverSupplies DNS replySends DNS answer
      

       Selected path
      

      Return path
      The reply goes back along the resolver connection. The DNS proxy checks it and returns it to the requesting resolver path. An application’s encrypted DNS session can bypass this query matcher.
      

      At the matcher
      The opt-in DNS proxy compares the question name against ordered rules. A rule can select resolver addresses or the original resolver. Forwarding uses the available TCP or UDP transport.
      Resolver reachability
      The route to the resolver IP determines the transport path. Choosing a resolver address alone cannot distinguish two VPNs that both use 10.0.0.53.
      After resolution
      The proxy checks the reply against the question. Exhausting the selected resolvers returns SERVFAIL. A later socket to an answer IP gets its own routing decision.

      Routing reference
      Where the routing rules live
      The SimpleVPN app validates the composition and installs capture settings through Network Extension. The system extension checks the installed configuration and owns the live multi-provider packet router. The UI can show a decision without handling the packet itself.
      Independent profiles can filter routes, DNS and proxy settings before they reach macOS. A route filter changes which prefixes a profile claims. A DNS or proxy filter changes a different system setting.
      What changes on the wire
      Consider an outbound TCP packet at the shared interface, 198.19.255.1:53120 → 10.42.8.19:443. If Lab assigned the Mac 10.99.0.2, the inner packet sent to Lab becomes 10.99.0.2:53120 → 10.42.8.19:443. WireGuard wraps it in encrypted UDP addressed to Lab’s public peer endpoint.
      On return, the matched reply destination changes from 10.99.0.2:53120 back to 198.19.255.1:53120. This is source NAT with reverse translation. The service’s real destination IP stays the same.
      Which clients can share an interface
      A shared destination-routed composition supports 2–16 single-peer WireGuard members. App or process routing supports 1–16. Each member has its own addresses, peer, keys and allowed destinations. Compatible resolver settings are required. App-routed members must agree on DNS servers and search domains.
      Other VPN kinds can use their supported independent connection paths. SSH forwards, a Proxy Tunnel and a native VPN each have their own entry points. Arbitrary VPN-over-VPN chaining is unavailable in this build.
      Which names affect a connection
      The live DNS proxy can choose a resolver for a question. A SOCKS client can hand a hostname to its proxy, and a PAC script can use a URL to choose a proxy. These are three separate decisions.
      The offline routing-language editor previews IP, app and process matches. Live WireGuard app rules are configured in Manage VPNs. DNS-to-process correlation, SNI steering, synthetic DNS with destination NAT and scripted FTP/SIP connection tracking are design work.
